    [Declaring the NAT64 prefixes](./config/config.md)).

- **Bun no longer fetches packages by name outside the lockfile.**

    Running a Bun command in a checkout where `bun install` had not been run let
    Bun's auto-install download any imported package straight from the registry by
    name, ignoring `bun.lock` — so neither the pinned versions nor their integrity
    hashes applied. Auto-install is now off in the engine and in each publication
    package: a missing install stops with `Cannot find package`, and dependencies
    come only from `bun install` against the lockfile.

- **A local certificate authority can now only certify the install's own addresses, and its site certificate can be renewed without touching the staff computers.**

    Every staff computer trusts the local certificate authority an install creates, and
    until now that authority could sign a certificate for any website: whoever obtained
    its key on the server could impersonate any site to those computers. A new authority
    is now restricted to the addresses it was issued for (the server name, any extra
    `--host` addresses, `localhost`) — exactly those names, not the names below them, so
    an authority for `museo.lan` cannot certify `mail.museo.lan` (a list where one name lies
    inside another is therefore refused) — and the key of the authority itself is deleted as
    soon as it has signed; the key that stays on the server can only sign under that
    restriction. The authority is also limited to website certificates, so that key cannot
    sign e-mail or software either.

    `deploy/dedalo-tls-rotate.sh` gains `--mode renew`: it re-issues the site certificate
    (now valid 397 days) from the same authority, so staff computers change nothing. It
    does nothing until the certificate is inside its last 30 days. On the Docker route,
    run it yourself once a year or from a monthly cron job (`docs/install/docker.md`,
    "Renewing the local-CA certificate"). `--host` can be given several times, for a LAN
    name or an IPv4 address beside the server name. When the new certificate is in place
    but the web server could not be reloaded (for example `docker` missing from cron's
    `PATH`), the script now exits with status 3 instead of reporting success, and every
    later run retries the reload until it works.

    An authority created before this change is not restricted. It keeps working and its
    certificate can be renewed (`--mode renew --host <name>`). Your next rotation
    (`--mode local-ca`) replaces it with a restricted one, which each staff computer then
    trusts in place of the old entry.

#### Changed

- **Ontology files move out of the code tree by default**

    Unset, `ONTOLOGY_DATA_IO_DIR` now resolves to `<private dir>/import/ontology`. The in-tree `install/import/ontology/` holds the release that ships with the code and is only read. Before, every install resolved to the in-tree directory, because the shipped release made it look non-empty. As a result, ontology updates wrote their staging files and recovery snapshots into the code tree, and the code updater refused every update with "Runtime data lives inside the code tree".

    An install whose in-tree directory holds anything that is not an ontology release file (a `recovery/` folder or `.staging` from an earlier update, any other file), or that is an ontology server, keeps that directory and logs a warning at start-up. Nothing is moved. The decision is taken once and recorded. The check goes by file name: an export of your own that carries a release file's name counts as release content. It can be rebuilt from the database, and a code update keeps it in the backup of the old code.

    Setting `ONTOLOGY_DATA_IO_DIR=` to an empty value now means the same as leaving it unset. Before, the code updater read the empty value as the code directory and refused.

    **One manual step for installs on an earlier release:** the refusal is checked by the code that is already running, so an existing install still refuses this update once. Before updating, run `mkdir <private dir>/import/ontology` as the service user. If you want to keep the old `install/import/ontology/7.0/recovery/` folder, move it there first.

    **On an ontology server, copy before you create.** It serves its exports from that directory, and the moment `<private dir>/import/ontology` exists it serves from there instead. Copy every `<major.minor>/` directory from `install/import/ontology/` into it, exports included, then restart. Never create the directory empty.

- **The installer field *Database role* is now *Database user*.**

    Same field, same value: the PostgreSQL user (a login role) Dédalo connects as and that
    owns the database — the name you pass to `psql -U`. The install summary says
    *database user* too. Nothing to change on an existing installation.

- **Dédalo prereleases are now published releases — from 7.0.0-beta.7 on, each beta is a fixed, signed version you can install and update.** *(action needed)*

    Until 7.0.0-beta.6, a beta was never published: its code reached an installation only
    as a developer build, and its Docker image only by building it yourself. From
    7.0.0-beta.7 on, every prerelease (`-alpha.N`, `-beta.N`, `-rc.N`) is published the way
    a release is, under its own name: a code archive with a checksum on the code server, and
    a signed official image `:7.0.0-beta.7`. Neither is ever rebuilt, so a bug report that
    names a prerelease names exact code. An installation is offered prereleases only when it
    chooses **Prereleases** (or **Developer builds**) in the *Update code* panel, and only
    from a code server that publishes them; the default, **Published releases**, never
    offers one.

    **Action needed** for an installation running 7.0.0-beta.6 or an earlier beta: it
    reports the bare version `7.0.0` and does not know about prereleases, so it is offered
    neither 7.0.0-beta.7 nor, later, 7.0.0. To move on:

    - a **Docker** installation updates its image to `7.0.0-beta.7`, as described in
      [a stack installed from a beta before 7.0.0-beta.7](./install/docker.md#a-stack-installed-from-a-beta-before-700-beta7);
    - an installation **updated from the panel** chooses **Developer builds** and installs
      the developer build of 7.0.0 the code server offers (see
      [testing development work on a real installation](./management/updates/updating_code.md#testing-development-work-on-a-real-installation)).
      With **Developer builds** still chosen, it is then
      offered every published build of 7.0.0 — 7.0.0-beta.7 and the later prereleases (from
      a code server that publishes prereleases), and 7.0.0 once it is released — because a
      developer build cannot tell which of them are older than it. Once it runs one of
      them, its panel's **Prereleases** and **Published releases** choices work as usual.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`, `WC-2026-09-29-code-release-channel-refs`.

- **The Docker and Trial installer installs the image of its own release — `7.0.0-beta.7` for a beta — and a stack built from an earlier beta needs `--skip-version-check` once on its next image update.** *(action needed)*

    The installer now knows which release it is from the git tag of the checkout or
    release archive it runs from, and says so in its header and on the System check:
    `7.0.0`, `7.0.0-beta.7 (prerelease)`, or `7.0.0.dev (development build)` for a
    commit with no release tag. That decides the image of a Docker or Trial install:

    - **A stable release or a prerelease** installs the image tagged with its own name.
      A beta asks the registry for `:7.0.0-beta.7`, never for `:7.0.0` — after the
      stable release that tag is a different image. The Review still asks the registry
      before `yes` and refuses an official image that is not published yet, with
      **Build** and **Custom** offered.
    - **A development build** has no official image: **Build** is preselected, and
      **Official** is refused on the Image screen without asking any registry.

    A local build is tagged and labelled with that name, and `.dedalo.env` pins it as
    `DEDALO_VERSION` (`7.0.0-beta.7`, or `7.0.0-dev` for a development build).

    The image updater (`deploy/dedalo-image-update.sh`) accepts prerelease versions and
    orders them as releases are ordered: `7.0.0-beta.6` < `7.0.0-beta.7` < `7.0.0-rc.1` <
    `7.0.0`. In `build` mode it checks out `v7.0.0-beta.7` for a prerelease (or the ref you
    name with `--ref`) and refuses a commit that is not that release — a tag that is not
    annotated, or names another version — before anything is built; a local build's version
    label is always what the engine inside it reports. `--skip-version-check` now also waives
    a step back within one data version, and never one to an older data version. A running
    engine that cannot read a prerelease version is asked about its data version instead
    (`7.0.0-dev` for `7.0.0-beta.7`), so a skipped `X.Y.Z` is still refused.

    **Action needed** for a stack installed from a beta up to 7.0.0-beta.6 with **Build**:
    it is pinned at the bare `DEDALO_VERSION=7.0.0`, and a prerelease comes before its
    stable release, so the move to `7.0.0-beta.7` reads as a downgrade. Its update script
    is still the old beta's, which refuses any prerelease version, so first move the
    stack's checkout to the new release (`git fetch --tags && git checkout v7.0.0-beta.7`),
    then run that one update with `--skip-version-check`; later updates need nothing. See
    [a stack installed from a beta before 7.0.0-beta.7](./install/docker.md#a-stack-installed-from-a-beta-before-700-beta7).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **A prerelease build now calls itself by its tag (`7.0.0-beta.7`), and its data version is published beside it.**

    Before, a build made from a beta tag reported the bare version of the release it
    precedes (`7.0.0`), so a beta could not be told apart from the stable release in
    `/health`, the About panels or the **Update code** panel. Now the program names
    itself by its git tag: `7.0.0` for a stable release, `7.0.0-beta.7` (or `-alpha.N`,
    `-rc.N`) for a prerelease, `7.0.0.dev` for any untagged build.

    The **data** version is unchanged and still the bare `7.0.0`: databases, updates and
    code servers keep comparing that. API consumers get it beside the name —
    `page_globals.dedalo_data_version`, and `/health` and the update status carry a new
    `release_kind` (`stable`, `prerelease` or `dev`) — so nothing needs to parse a
    version out of the name. A beta asking a code server for updates keeps sending the
    bare data version, which every code server, older ones included, understands.

    A code server reads the release name from the tag when it builds an archive, which
    needs **git 2.35 or newer** on the code server: with an older git, *Build release*
    now refuses (before, the archive was built and every installation of it called
    itself a developer build).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

#### Added

- **The profile tool-permissions panel explains each tool — an info button unfolds its description.**

    In a profile's **Tool permissions** field, every tool row now carries a small info button. It unfolds the tool's
    description (in the interface language) under the row and folds it again on a second click, so the panel stays
    compact while an administrator decides which tools to grant. Tools without a description show no button.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-tool-permissions-description`.

- **"A code server can publish a prerelease (`Build prerelease`), and a published release is never rebuilt."**

    The *serve code* panel has a third button, *Build prerelease*, beside *Build release*.
    It builds the newest prerelease tag (for example `v7.0.1-beta.2`) that is newer than the
    newest release tag, into `<X>/<X.Y>/7.0.1-beta.2.zip` with its `.sha256` file. The
    *Prerelease tag* row names the tag before you press the button. When there is no such
    tag, the row says so and offers no button. *Build release* still builds only stable
    `vX.Y.Z` tags.

    A built release or prerelease cannot be built again. If its `.zip` and `.sha256` are
    already on disk, the build is refused and the files are not changed. To publish
    different code, tag a new release. Before the code server publishes an archive, it
    checks that the archive gives the tag's name as its version. A tag made without `-a`
    (a lightweight tag) fails this check, so the build is refused. A prerelease tag made
    before this check existed (up to `v7.0.0-beta.6`) cannot pass it either, so the panel
    does not offer it; the first prerelease that can be built is one tagged after it.

    For developers: the pre-push hook now refuses a lightweight release tag. It also asks
    for a full green gate for a prerelease tag, in the same way as for a stable tag.
    `bun run push:release-tag` now takes the pushed tag object as a third argument.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **"Code updates move between prereleases of one version: beta to later beta, beta to its release."**

    An installation that runs a prerelease can now install a later prerelease of the same
    version, or that version's release, from the *Update code* panel or with
    `deploy/dedalo-image-update.sh`: `7.0.0-beta.6` → `7.0.0-beta.7` → `7.0.0-rc.1` →
    `7.0.0`. These moves need no data update, and prereleases may be skipped. Moving back
    (`7.0.0-beta.7` → `7.0.0-beta.6`, or from `7.0.0` to one of its prereleases) is refused.
    A move to the next version still goes one version at a time; its data update runs once,
    on the first build of that version you install.

    A prerelease needs the *Prereleases* (or *Developer builds*) choice of the panel. On a
    container installation the panel can now request a prerelease image too, and the running
    engine checks a prerelease version itself instead of refusing it as malformed.

    After the restart, the panel reports an update as landed only when the server answers
    with the exact version it installed; a server that answers with another build of the
    same version is reported as rolled back.

    An update is refused, before anything is swapped, when the archive it would download is not
    the release it names, or when the downloaded archive calls itself another release.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **"Prereleases have an official image: `:7.0.1-beta.2`, signed, and never under a release's tag."**

    Pushing a prerelease tag (for example `v7.0.1-beta.2`) now publishes the official Docker
    image `:7.0.1-beta.2`, in the same way as a release: built from the tag's code, signed,
    with the same digest in every registry, and never rebuilt once published. The image is
    published only under its own name. It never replaces `:7.0.1`, which is the image of the
    release, and no image is tagged `latest`, `7` or `7.0`.

    So the installer of a prerelease can now use the **Official** image: it asks the registry
    for `:7.0.1-beta.2`, and finds it once the image is published.

    The signature check accepts prerelease tags. If you verify images by hand with
    `cosign verify`, use the identity printed in the Docker installation guide, which now
    includes them. The old command still verifies release images, but it refuses a prerelease
    image.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **"The update panel can ask for prereleases: choose published releases, prereleases or developer builds."**

    The *Developer builds* checkbox of the *Update code* panel is now a choice of three:
    **Published releases** (the default), **Prereleases** and **Developer builds**. Each
    choice also offers what the one before it offers. A prerelease (for example
    `7.0.1-beta.2`) is a fixed, checksum-verified build of a version that is not yet stable,
    and its row shows that full version. An installation that asks for published releases
    is never offered a prerelease.

    A code server offers prereleases only when it sets the new
    `DEDALO_CODE_SERVER_PRERELEASE_CHANNEL=true`, which is separate from
    `DEDALO_CODE_SERVER_DEV_CHANNEL`. When the code server does not offer part of what you
    chose (it is not set up for it, or it runs an older Dédalo version), it lists only what it
    does offer and the panel names the missing part above the list.

    An installation that runs a prerelease is also shown the later prereleases and the
    release of its own version, and can install them (see the entry on moving between
    prereleases).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **The production installer can now make a local certificate authority, for an intranet with no public name.**

    A museum that installs Dédalo with internet access and then runs it on an isolated
    intranet has no public name, so Let's Encrypt cannot reach it, and until now the only
    other choice on the production route was to make certificates by hand. The *Web server
    & TLS* screen now offers **Local CA** (`--tls local_ca`), as the Docker route already
    did. **Other addresses** (`--tls-extra-names dedalo.lan,archivo.museo.lan`) adds the
    other names staff type: the certificate names them and the site answers to them.

    On an intranet with no local DNS, **Other addresses** can also list the server's IPv4
    addresses (`--tls-extra-names dedalo.lan,192.168.1.20`), on both routes: staff then open
    `https://192.168.1.20/`, and `http://` to it redirects to `https://`. A browser sends no
    server name for an IP address, so on the production route the instance *claims* the
    address in the installer's host-wide catch-all, which hands a handshake to that address
    the instance's certificate. Every other site on the server keeps answering by name, on
    that address too, and a handshake to an address no instance claims is refused as
    before. The System check refuses an address that is not this server's, one another
    instance already claims, one a site of yours listens on itself, a site of yours on port
    443 that loads before the catch-all (it would answer visits by IP address), and IPv6. On nginx the
    claiming instance's site key becomes readable by the web server's group, because nginx
    loads that certificate per connection; on Apache, one instance per server can claim
    addresses. See [Reaching an instance by IP address](./install/reverse_proxy.md#reaching-an-instance-by-ip-address).

    The installer makes the authority and the site certificate in
    `/opt/dedalo/instances/<i>/tls/`, with the same script the Docker route and every
    rotation use. The authority can only certify the install's own addresses, exactly. When the
    install ends, the *To do on this host* list names the authority's file and its SHA-256
    fingerprint, how to trust it once on Windows, macOS, Linux and Firefox, and the `curl`
    command that checks it from a staff computer. The site certificate then renews itself
    from the same authority (`dedalo-tls-renew@<i>.timer`), so staff computers never trust
    anything again. `--abort` removes only what this install made: the timer, its drop-in
    and the certificate directory.

    On both routes, an install over a certificate directory that already holds an authority
    stops at the *System check* when that authority cannot serve the answered addresses,
    and names the rotation command. That happens when it was made for other addresses, or
    when it was made before this release and its certificate does not name them all. The
    production route also refuses an authority made before this release, because it is not
    restricted. See [Production install](./install/production.md); its last section is a
    recipe for trying the production route in a virtual machine with no domain name.

#### Fixed

- **Aborting an install (`--abort`) no longer fails with a deadlock when something else is connected to its database.**

    When `--abort` (or a reinstall over an aborted install) resets the install's database, any
    other session still connected to that database — a server left running, an open `psql`, a
    monitoring tool — could hold a table the reset had to drop. The reset then failed with
    `deadlock detected`, or waited indefinitely behind a session idle in a transaction.

    The reset now ends every other session on **that database only** (never another database,
    never the installer's own lock) before it starts, waits until they are gone, and runs again
    when the server still picks it as a deadlock victim or a lock wait times out — up to four
    times, each attempt one transaction that rolls back whole. If it still cannot finish, it
    stops with a line naming the reason and any session the installer's database role is not
    allowed to end ([Troubleshooting](./install/troubleshooting.md)); when it completes despite
    such a session, its result line names that session too.

- **The installer no longer crashes when a check's helper process stops before reading its request.**

    Each installer check (System, database, mail, …) runs in a helper process of its own. If that
    process stopped before reading what it was asked to check — failing at start, or stopped at its
    time limit — the installer itself could exit with a "broken pipe" error. The check now simply
    fails, with a sentence saying the helper did not read its request, and the installer stays open.

- **A maintenance job whose progress cannot be followed now says so instead of waiting forever.**

    When the progress of a long job (a backup, a code update, a move of terms or languages) could
    not be followed at all — the connection failed, the server refused the request, or it answered
    without any content — the panel kept showing what it showed before, and a move whose run could
    not be followed kept its form locked ("an execute is still running") until the page was
    reloaded. The panel now states the failure inside the panel, with the request id to look up in
    the server log, and the form is released. A refusal there never turns the whole page into an
    error page.

- **The publication host's `install.sh` no longer hangs on a stalled Bun download.**

    Before, `install.sh` downloaded Bun with a size limit only: a mirror (or GitHub) that accepted the
    connection and then stopped answering — during the TLS handshake or mid-download — left the
    install waiting forever, holding its lock. Now every download has a connect deadline and a total
    deadline; when one passes, `install.sh` stops with a line saying so and naming the ways on
    (retry, `--mirror <https base url>`, or `--offline <bun zip>`). See the
    [publication host guide](./install/publication_host.md).

- **Installing or resetting a thesaurus no longer waits without limit behind another session's lock**

    **Maintenance › Install hierarchies** (both **Install** and **Reset to seed**) imports
    a thesaurus in one transaction. If another session held a lock on one of its terms
    (for example, an editor's unfinished save, or a database session left idle in a
    transaction), the import waited for that lock with no limit. While it waited, it kept
    the terms it had already reached locked, so edits to those terms queued behind it,
    and nothing could stop it. Now each lock wait gives up after 5 seconds, the same limit
    every other maintenance operation uses, and the whole import is retried a few times.
    If the lock is still held, the import stops with a message saying that another
    session holds a lock on the thesaurus. Nothing is changed, and you can run it again
    once the lock is released. If the import is stopped, it ends at once and nothing is
    changed. The result names any case where it could not confirm whether the import
    was applied.

- **The publication-marker index is now repaired every 10 minutes as well as at startup, and a repair held off by a running publication is retried instead of skipped.**

    The web server decides whether anonymous visitors may open a record's media by a marker the engine keeps in `.publication/pub`. That set is re-derived from the per-publication truth after every start, to repair a marker pair a crash left half-written. When a publication was writing at that moment for longer than two minutes, the repair was skipped and not tried again until the next restart, so a published record's media could stay unreachable — or a withdrawn one stay public — for as long as the server kept running. The repair is now retried a minute later until it completes, and it also runs every 10 minutes, which heals a pair left half-written by a publication process that died while the server stayed up. The periodic repair holds the publication targets only when it actually has something to repair, and when it did hold them it then completes the removals of records deleted meanwhile, so a record deleted while it ran leaves the public site with that run instead of waiting for the next publication. In the maintenance area, **Reconcile** shows the schedule as `boot + every 10 min` and marks a run that had to wait as *DEFERRED*, with the reason; `GET /api/v1/counters` carries it as `last_deferred`.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-22-reconcile-deferred-rearm`.

- **A running move execute in Maintenance can no longer be hidden by a new Preview**

    In the five Maintenance move widgets (move languages, locators, TLD, to portal, to
    table), clicking **Preview** while an **Execute** was still running replaced the
    execute's progress panel and the record that lets a reloaded page find it again.
    The result of the execute (completed, rolled back, partly applied, or unknown) was
    never shown, so it was easy to run the same move a second time. While an execute
    runs, **Preview** and **Execute** now explain why they wait instead of starting a
    new run. A reloaded page reconnects to a running execute and keeps it in front.
    If the server did not confirm an execute, the widget waits for a page reload
    before it starts another run.

- **The publication host installer never puts a cut-off file in place on a full disk**

    When the disk of a publication host was nearly full, the root provisioner
    could write only part of a systemd unit, an environment file, a sudoers or
    polkit rule, or the copied Bun binary. It then moved that cut-off file into
    place and reported the step as done. A short write is now continued until
    every byte is on disk. If the disk is really full, the step fails, the old
    file stays where it was and no temporary file is left behind.

    Cursor keys pressed at a guided-install prompt no longer leave stray
    characters such as `[D` in the answer.

- **An archive restore refuses an ontology node another writer created between the plan and the write**

    A restore plans its ontology definitions first and writes them later. A definition another writer created in between used to be overwritten silently, as if it were new. The plan is now checked again at the moment of writing: an identical definition is left alone, and a different one is refused unless the restore was asked to overwrite conflicts. The restore's report now counts what was actually written.

- **An archive restore no longer plants ontology definitions that the next ontology rebuild would delete**

    An archive carries the ontology definitions of its sections, but not the ontology records they are built from. Restoring it into an installation whose ontology already has records for the same TLD used to add those definitions anyway: the next ontology update (or a rebuild from the ontology parser tool) removed them again, and the restored records were left without their definitions. The restore now refuses this case before writing anything, and names the TLD and the definitions involved. Install or update that ontology so that it defines them, then run the restore again: the definitions are then found unchanged, or the conflict is named. A TLD for which this installation has no ontology records restores as before. The restore also waits for any ontology rebuild of the same TLD that is in progress, instead of writing at the same time. See [The archive door](./core/exporting_data.md#the-archive-door).

- **A backup's verification proof now survives a power cut, and a backup is reported done only once its name is safely on disk.**

    When a backup is verified, Dédalo writes a small proof file next to it so the archive is not read in full again. That proof could be lost in a power cut right after the verification, or left half-written by an interrupted write, and the next check then re-read the whole archive. It is now written through the same durable path as every other engine file: complete, synced, and its name synced too. If the disk refuses to make a finished backup's name durable (an I/O error), the backup job now says it failed instead of reporting it done; the backup file itself is kept.

- **Code updates of a git-checkout install no longer refuse over `.claude` and `CLAUDE.md`**

    An install made with `git clone` holds two files that no release ships, `.claude` and `CLAUDE.md`. The code updater saw them as unknown files and refused every update with "Unknown entries at the code-tree root". The updater now reads the files a release leaves out from the release's own `.gitattributes`. Those files move into the backup with the old code, and the update proceeds.

    **One manual step for checkout installs on an earlier release:** the refusal is checked by the code that is already running, so the next update still refuses once. Before updating, delete the two links from the install directory: `rm .claude CLAUDE.md`. They are tracked by git, so `git checkout -- .claude CLAUDE.md` restores them.

- **An update or a move transform that committed after a lost connection says what did not run**

    If the database connection fails while a data update or a *move* transform file is
    being committed, Dédalo asks the database whether the work committed and reports it as
    applied when it did. Some follow-up actions only run after a commit Dédalo saw
    succeed, such as updating dependent fields and ending the sessions of users whose
    access changed. In this case they were skipped without a word. The report now says
    that they did not run and what to do: run the *observer_mirrors* reconcile (an update
    starts one itself), and end the sessions of any account whose access the change
    affected.

- **An export's record selection now respects the database statement ceiling.**

    With `DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS` set, computing an export's record selection could still run
    far past it: PostgreSQL lifts the statement ceiling at the moment it builds the selection.
    Now the selection runs under the same ceiling as every other request: an export whose
    selection takes longer to compute is stopped at the ceiling with `db.statement_timeout`,
    before its first line, and its database connection is freed. Installations that keep the
    default `0` (no ceiling) see no change.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-export-buffered-cap-and-admission`.

- **A lookup in an external catalogue now always ends within its timeout, even when the name server or the answer stalls.**

    The timeout of an external record service (for example Zenon) started only when the
    connection was opened. Resolving the service's name, and reading an answer that stopped
    arriving, were not covered, so a stalled name server or a stalled answer could keep the
    lookup — and one of the service's few parallel request slots — waiting indefinitely. The
    whole request, from the name lookup to the last byte of the answer, is now covered by the
    service's configured timeout, and such a request is reported as timed out.

- **Exporting a thesaurus never leaves or certifies a partial dump**

    The hierarchy export panel used to stream each thesaurus straight to its final file and judge the export by "the file exists". A dump cut short (a server error, a dropped connection, a full disk) still left a valid-looking file, and `hierarchy.json` then certified it with a checksum, so an installation importing it received a partial thesaurus. Each dump is now written beside its final name and moved into place only when psql succeeded, the file reads to its end, and it holds exactly the rows psql reported; otherwise the panel names the reason and the previous good file is kept. Building `hierarchy.json` also refuses, keeping the previous manifest, when a data file it would list is torn or changed while it was built. A complete but short dump left by an export made before this fix cannot be told apart: export those thesauri again.

- **Installer and container fixes — `--abort` removals survive a power cut, a half-imported thesaurus is no longer reported installed, the published client never points at a missing copy**

    - **`--abort` survives a power cut.** When the installer takes back what it wrote — the
      `.env` it created, its backups and staged copies of the secrets, and its own run record —
      the removals are now forced to disk before it reports *aborted*. Before, a power cut right
      after could bring those files back: the database password on disk again, or a run record
      that `--resume` took for a live install.
    - **A thesaurus whose models never landed is no longer "already installed".** When the terms
      of a thesaurus are in the database but a section its release ships data for (typically the
      models) is empty, installing it again used to answer *already installed — skipped*, and
      the missing section never arrived. It is now refused with a line naming the empty section
      and *Reset to seed* (*Maintenance → Install hierarchies*), which imports the whole
      thesaurus; nothing is written by the refusal.
    - **Container stacks: the client copy is replaced without a gap.** When the engine
      republishes a damaged copy of the client at start-up, the new copy now gets its own
      directory and the web server is switched to it in one step. Before, there was a short
      window — and, after a power cut there, a lasting one until the next start — in which the
      web server pointed at a copy that was not there.
    - **The installer's ontology step says what it checked.** Downloaded ontology files are
      checked for their format, over a verified connection to the configured ontology server;
      the master server does not publish digests to check them against. The step now reports
      them as *shape-checked*, not *verified*.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-hierarchy-import-partial-refused`.

- **The installer's configuration and the published client now survive a power cut**

    Three install and start-up writes were safe against a crashed process but not against
    a power cut or a kernel crash.

    - **The `.env` the installer writes** (the only copy of the generated salt and the
      database password) is now forced to disk before the installer records that step as
      done. So is the pre-install backup that `--abort` restores, and so is the restored
      file itself. Before, a power cut could bring the `.env` back empty while the
      installer's own record said it had been written. A failed write no longer leaves a
      staged copy of the secrets next to it either.
    - **The client a container publishes for nginx** is now written to disk in full before
      the switch to it. At every start the engine also re-checks the published files
      against the client it runs, so a copy damaged by a power cut is republished instead
      of being served until the next update. A republish no longer empties the live copy
      first, which used to cause a short burst of 404s.
    - **The seed restore** no longer passes the database dump through a predictable file
      name in the shared temporary directory. Before, another local user on a multi-user
      Linux host could plant that file and add SQL to what the installer ran. The dump now
      goes to a fresh private directory.

- **The temporary audio copy made for on-premise transcription is deleted as soon as it has been sent.**

    Automatic transcription with the institution's own recognition server makes a temporary
    speech-quality copy of the interview and sends its bytes to that server. The copy used to
    be deleted only when the background check of the transcription finished, so it stayed on
    disk when the submission failed, when the check never ran (the job was stopped while
    waiting, or the server restarted) or when the check could not be scheduled. It is now
    deleted the moment the submission ends, whatever its outcome.

- **Interrupted exports and transcriptions no longer leave temporary files behind**

    A thesaurus export stopped mid-dump (the server killed or restarted) left a
    `<tipo>.copy.gz.tmp-…` or `hierarchy.json.tmp-…` file in `install/import/hierarchy`
    for good. The next export now removes such leftovers once they are more than six hours
    old; a newer one, which may belong to an export still running, is kept. Building
    `hierarchy.json` also checks each data file in one streamed pass instead of reading
    whole dumps into memory. A background transcription that failed with an unexpected
    error kept its temporary copy of the recording on disk; the copy is now removed however
    the job ends.

- **Deleting or restoring an ontology record now removes or restores its runtime node.**

    Deleting an ontology record (or emptying its data) left its node in the runtime ontology, still
    served everywhere; restoring a deleted record from the Time Machine brought the record back
    without its node. Both now move the node with the record, in the same transaction. A local
    override follows the same rule: deleting or restoring it re-applies the node it overrides.
    Writing a record's content into the runtime ontology stays a developer action: when a user who
    is not a developer restores a record, or deletes or restores an override, the record changes
    but the node does not, and the ontology inspection lists it as drift for a developer to apply.
    The same holds when no user is identified at all (for example a write through the stdio MCP
    server): only a developer's action writes node content.
    An ontology rebuild, a registry activation and a record delete or restore on the same TLD no
    longer race each other, and activating a TLD while it is being deleted no longer leaves its root
    node behind.
    See [Ontology write pipeline](./core/ontology/ontology_write.md).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-record-lifecycle`.

- **Building the ontology recovery file no longer stops the server when the disk is full, and the file survives a power cut**

    The ontology recovery file (*Maintenance → Build database version*) is the safety net an
    ontology update relies on.

    - **A full disk or a read-only private directory** while the file was being written used
      to stop the whole server process, or leave the request waiting forever. The build now
      fails like any other failed build: it reports the error, keeps the previous recovery
      file as it was, and leaves no partial file behind.
    - **A power cut right after a successful build** could leave an empty or partial recovery
      file under its final name. The file is now forced to disk before it replaces the
      previous one, and so is the replacement itself.

- **The ontology status panel reports a TLD shown under the wrong typology, and the hierarchy typology groups are filed where the master ontology files them**

    In the ontology tree, each TLD hangs under the typology set in its registry record. A TLD placed under a different typology used to be reported as in sync. The ontology status panel now reports it as drift, and **Rebuild** puts it back under the right typology. Separately, the first time a thesaurus is created, Dédalo registers the `hierarchytype` and `hierarchymtype` groups itself, because no ontology update brings them in. It used to file them under *Core*, with generic names. It now uses the typology and names that the master ontology gives them. Installations that registered these groups before this change keep their current placement, which stays consistent and is not reported as drift.

- **The installer's downloaded ontology files survive a power cut**

    The installer fetches the chosen ontology files before it touches the database, and
    records that step as done. The files were not forced to disk, so a power cut right
    after that step could lose them, and resuming the installation then refused with a
    "changed outside the installer" error that only recreating the installation would
    clear. The files and their checklist are now written to disk safely before the step
    counts as done, and each file appears under its final name only once it has been
    checked.

- **An ontology update now removes the nodes a new package no longer carries.**

    Before, **Update ontology** only added and refreshed nodes: a node dropped upstream stayed in the
    runtime ontology for good, and a record whose TLD field named another TLD was silently written
    into that other TLD. Each updated TLD is now re-derived in one transaction by the same writer the
    ontology parser uses: dropped nodes go, a misfiled record is skipped and named in the update's
    warnings, and the nodes that remain keep their internal ids. A model that the update adds or
    renames now reaches every component that uses it in the same update, including components in
    another updated TLD. A typology grouper that this installation created (for a thesaurus or TLD
    of a typology the release does not ship) is kept: the update re-creates its record instead of
    removing it, so the thesauri under it stay in the ontology tree. See
    [Ontology write pipeline](./core/ontology/ontology_write.md).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-update-rebuild`.

- **Phantom-language removal and the public-tier reconcile no longer hang on a busy publication target**

    Removing phantom publication languages and applying the public-tier reconcile
    used to wait without limit while a publication run held the target database.
    They now wait at most 2 minutes in total, then report the busy target and leave
    it untouched: re-run the action when the publication run has finished.

    The publication-host kit (`hostagent:pack`) is now written durably, and a failed
    pack no longer leaves a temporary file beside it.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-09-30-diffusion-target-fence`.

- **A publication run or unpublish no longer waits without limit on a lock held outside Dédalo**

    Publishing to a MariaDB database waited as long as MariaDB let it (a day, by
    default) when another session held a lock on the table — for example a long read
    on the public website while a run added a column. Meanwhile every other
    publication to that database waited too, and deleted records stayed published.
    Now a statement waits at most 30 seconds for such a lock: the run fails and
    releases the database (re-run it), a deleted record's unpublish stays pending and
    is retried, and the language sweep and the media-index rebuild report the table.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-target-statement-lock-wait`.

- **The Reconcile panel offers *Apply* only where you can apply, and a refusal no longer replaces the page**

    In *Maintenance → Reconcile*, every row showed an *Apply* button. Two of them could not
    work for most people: *media_copy* applies only for the root user, and *publication_apis*
    never applies there at all (Publication API code is pushed from the publication-hosts
    panel). Clicking either one showed the no-access page in place of the panel.

    Now each row knows who may apply it. Where you cannot, *Apply* is disabled and its tooltip
    says why. *Check* (the dry run) works as before on every row.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-09-03-maintenance-reconcile-status-widget`.

- **New installations and imported thesauri store record references in their final form**

    Every reference from one record to another names the target record by number. Dédalo
    stores that number as a number, but a fresh installation was born with thousands of
    references written as text (the administrator account's profile and project, the
    languages, the core ontology), and installing or resetting a thesaurus from
    *Maintenance › Install hierarchies* copied the text form of the vendored files as it
    was. Searches matched both forms, so nothing looked wrong, but the text form is what
    the planned clean-up of old installations removes. Now a new installation and every
    thesaurus you install or reset store numbers only, and a new installation records that
    its data is already in the final form. Nothing else in the data changes.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-seed-and-thesaurus-int-clean`.

- **Installing or resetting a thesaurus takes effect at once and no longer needs gigabytes of memory**

    After *Maintenance › Install hierarchies* installed a thesaurus, or *Reset to seed*
    replaced its terms, lists and counts built from those terms could keep showing the old
    terms until the server was restarted: deleted terms were still offered and edited
    labels still shown. They now refresh as soon as the import finishes.

    The import also no longer loads whole thesaurus files into the server's memory. The
    largest vendored thesaurus is about one gigabyte once unpacked, and the server needed
    more than two gigabytes to import it, enough to be stopped on a modest machine with
    every user's request lost. It now reads the files piece by piece. A file that changes
    on disk while it is being imported is refused, and nothing of that thesaurus is
    changed.

    A reset still does not rebuild what other parts of Dédalo derived from the deleted
    terms. The result message now says so and names what to run afterwards: the
    *observer_mirrors* reconcile, and a new publication or semantic-search reconcile if
    the thesaurus is published or indexed.

- **Time machine restores respect every record's projects and every field's permission; the ontology recovery file is built one at a time**

    - **Reverting a bulk change never brings back a record outside your projects.** When a
      revert re-links a record that an earlier revert deleted, that record is now checked
      against your projects like any other. If it is outside them, that change is skipped as
      *out of scope* and the record stays deleted.
    - **Restoring a field's history needs permission on its dataframe too.** *Apply value* in
      the time machine also rewrites the dataframe attached to the field, such as roles or
      ratings. It now needs edit permission on that dataframe as well. A user who can only
      read the dataframe gets a permission error, and nothing is restored.
    - **One recovery-file build or restore at a time.** In *Maintenance → Build database
      version*, a second build or restore of the ontology recovery file started while one is
      running is refused with *already running*. Before, two at once could leave a damaged
      recovery file behind a success message.
    - **An ontology update that has finished is not undone by a late error.** If a final
      report step of *Update ontology* fails after the new ontology is in place, the update
      stays in place. The message now says that the update landed and that nothing was rolled
      back.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-tm-restore-component-write-doors`, `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-recovery-single-flight`.

- **Restoring a whole record from the time machine needs permission on every field it changes; a failed ontology re-index after an update no longer brings the old ontology back**

    - **Restoring a whole record checks every field it changes.** *Apply value* on a whole
      record in the time machine now needs edit permission on each field the restore would
      change, like restoring a single field already does. A user who manages user accounts can
      no longer give their own account back an earlier profile or administrator flag this way,
      and a field you may only read is never rewritten by a restore. A refused restore changes
      nothing. Undeleting a record works as before.
    - **An ontology update whose re-indexing fails keeps the new ontology.** If *Update
      ontology* has imported the new ontology but rebuilding the ontology tree from it fails,
      the update now stays in place and the message names the ontologies to rebuild in
      *Maintenance*. Before, the old ontology was put back under a tree already partly rebuilt
      from the new one.
    - **A stuck recovery-file build no longer blocks the next one.** Building or restoring the
      ontology recovery file in *Maintenance → Build database version* now gives up after ten
      minutes and reports it, instead of waiting forever and refusing every later attempt as
      *already running*.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-tm-section-restore-write-door`, `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-update-derive-landed`, `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-recovery-deadline`.

- **Unpublished media stays unpublished after a power cut — and is never reported withdrawn while it is still served**

    - **A power cut can no longer bring back the media of a withdrawn record.** When a record is
      deleted or unpublished, the markers that let the web server serve its media files
      anonymously are now forced to disk before the record is reported unpublished. Before, a
      power cut right after could restore them, and the next start-up re-derived public access
      from them — with nothing left to retry the withdrawal.
    - **A withdrawal that could not remove the markers stays pending.** If the media markers of
      an unpublished record cannot be removed (a permission problem on the media store, a full
      disk), the unpublish is now kept *pending* and retried, instead of being recorded as
      *unpublished* over media that is still public.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-unpublish-markers-durable`.

- **Rebuilding or updating one user's activity statistics never counts a day twice**

    Two rebuilds of the same user's activity statistics running at once, or a rebuild and an update, could each save the same day, so that day's totals appeared twice. Every writer of one user's statistics now waits for the other, and a day already saved is never saved again.

- **Docker stacks — ontology update no longer fails with EACCES**

    Both Docker stacks now set `ONTOLOGY_DATA_IO_DIR=/private/import/ontology`. Before this, the engine fell back to the in-tree `install/import/ontology`, which is root-owned in the image, so **Maintenance → Update ontology** died with `EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '…/install/import/ontology/7.0/.staging'`. Existing installs pick this up from the updated compose file: `docker compose up -d` recreates the engine container, and no manual `chown` is needed.

- **The installer says what to do when the checkout's dependencies are missing.**

    `bun run scripts/install.ts` in a checkout where `bun install` had not been run
    stopped at once with `Cannot find package 'zod'`, which named neither the cause
    nor the fix. It now refuses with one sentence: run `bun install` in the checkout
    first. Nothing is written. `sh install.sh` is unchanged and still installs the
    dependencies itself. See
    [Running the installer without `install.sh`](./install/installer_reference.md#running-the-installer-without-installsh).

- **A code update that is refused says so once, not three times**

    When an update could not start — no maintenance mode, no recent backup, a bad checksum — the **Update code** panel printed the same refusal in three places at once: a generic "Process 2" line, a red banner that floated over the list of update steps, and the panel's own notice underneath. The steps list also stayed on screen with every phase marked "Pending", which read as an update that was stuck rather than one that never started.

    Now the panel states the refusal in one place, in the interface language, and nothing floats over the panel. The progress list is kept only when something actually ran; a run that fails part-way still shows which step failed, once.

### For developers

#### Security

- **The component lock requests refuse a section that is not an ontology tipo.**

    `dd_utils_api` `update_lock_components_state` and `get_lock_status` now check that
    `options.section_tipo` is a string in the tipo grammar before doing anything, for every
    action — including the caller's own lock cleanup, which runs no section read check. A missing
    value still answers `400 request.invalid_options`; a present value that is not a tipo (an array,
    an object, a number, a free string) now answers `400 request.invalid_tipo` and touches no lock,
    where it used to reach the database as-is. The Dédalo client always sends a tipo, so nothing
    changes for it.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-23-lock-section-tipo-grammar`.

#### Changed

- **"Build database version: the install-seed build's answer and panel values are documented"**

    *Maintenance → Build database version → Build install version* compiles the install seed
    from the repository's own sources (since 7.0.0-beta.6). Its answer (the step readout and file size on success; a `maintenance.action_failed`
    error carrying the same readout on a refusal) and the panel's three values (now the seed
    sources, the scratch database pattern and the seed file, never the installation's database
    name) are now recorded in the wire contract, for anyone scripting against the maintenance
    API.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-09-build-install-version-owned-mode`.

- **A developer install gets its own unix socket, named after its entity, and is refused while another server holds it.**

    **One socket per checkout.** The developer route used to write no `SERVER_UNIX_SOCKET`,
    so every checkout on a machine listened on `/tmp/dedalo_ts.sock`, and a second one could
    not start. The Development server screen now asks for the socket and always writes it.
    The default carries the entity: entity `test` gets `/tmp/dedalo_ts_test.sock`. Change it
    there or with `--socket`. On a re-run, the socket your `.env` already names is kept.

    **Refused before anything is written.** When a running server already answers on the
    chosen socket (another checkout's `bun run dev`), the Review refuses to install, and so
    does a headless run, before it writes anything. Before, that only failed at the
    installer's last step, after the install was sealed. A leftover socket file that nothing
    answers on is not refused; the server removes it when it starts. A socket path longer
    than 103 bytes (the operating system's limit) is refused on any route. See the
    [developer quickstart](./install/dev_quickstart.md#7-run-it).

- **"`page_globals` now says what kind of build is running (`release_kind`), and the harvesting user agent names the release."**

    `page_globals` has a new key, `release_kind`: `stable`, `prerelease` or `dev`, the same
    values as `/health`. Like `dedalo_version`, it is `null` for a visitor who is not
    logged in. The version badge in the menu's debug bar uses it. It shows `beta` for a
    prerelease and `dev` for an untagged build. Before, the badge said `beta` for every
    `7.0` version, including the stable release.

    The `User-Agent` header sent by the harvesting tools now carries the release name,
    for example `dedalo/7.0.0-beta.7 (+https://dedalo.dev; heritage cataloguing)`. Before,
    it carried the bare data version (`dedalo/7.0.0`). The `dedalo` token that a
    `robots.txt` group addresses is unchanged.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-15-release-identity-from-tag`.

- **A developer install is reported complete only once `bun run dev` has served, and it ends by saying where to open it.**

    **Served, then complete.** A developer install used to end with "install complete"
    without anything having served the browser. Its last step, `verify_dev_server`, now
    starts `bun run dev` once with the `.env` the install wrote, asks the development
    listener for `/health` over HTTPS (the local certificate authority as the trust
    anchor), logs in as `root` over it (every cookie the login sets must be `Secure` exactly
    when the listener is HTTPS), and stops it again. It refuses to run as root in a
    checkout another user owns. If it fails, the install is not reported complete and
    the message names the cause: the port taken by another program, a certificate the
    server cannot read or that does not verify, the database unreachable, a
    development dependency missing, another Dédalo server on the same unix socket, a
    cookie flag that does not match the listener, or the login refused. The install is
    sealed by then, so the message names the key to edit in the written `.env`
    (`SERVER_TCP_PORT`, `SERVER_UNIX_SOCKET`) rather than an installer flag, and the
    failure hint no longer offers `--abort`. Fix it and run the installer with
    `--resume`, which runs the check again. An install written to another private
    directory is started, and shown, as `DEDALO_PRIVATE_DIR=<dir> bun run dev`.

    **Where to open it.** The installer then ends with what to do next, built from the
    keys it wrote: `bun run dev`, every address the client answers on
    (`https://127.0.0.1:3500/dedalo/core/page/` and `https://localhost:3500/…` with the
    defaults, plus this machine's network addresses when it is opened to the network),
    the `root` login, and the certificate authority's path, SHA-256 fingerprint and
    whether this machine trusts it. The full-screen installer leaves these lines on the
    terminal when it closes. See the
    [developer quickstart](./install/dev_quickstart.md#5-run-the-installer).

    **`bun run dev` stops when its CSS watcher dies.** The stylesheet watcher never
    stops on a LESS error, so when it exits something is wrong — usually a missing
    development dependency (`Cannot find package 'less'`). `bun run dev` now stops with
    it and says so, instead of serving on while every stylesheet edit is lost.

#### Added

- **A developer install now issues the development listener's HTTPS certificate and makes this machine trust it; `bun run tls:renew` and `bun run tls:untrust` manage it afterwards.**

    **The certificate.** With the default `--tls local_ca`, the developer route issues
    the development listener's certificate with the same generator the other routes use
    (`deploy/dedalo-tls-rotate.sh`), into `<private>/tls`, as the checkout's owner. Its
    certificate authority can certify only `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and, when the
    listener is opened to the network, the IPv4 address it binds (or this machine's IPv4
    network addresses with `0.0.0.0`). IPv6 addresses are not certified: a listener on
    this machine is opened as `https://localhost:…`, which the certificate names, and a
    specific IPv6 `--dev-host` with `local_ca` is refused. A re-run keeps the authority
    and renews its certificate when it has less than 30 days left. An authority made
    for other addresses is refused before anything is written, and the refusal names
    the command that replaces it.

    **Trust.** The installer prints the authority's path and SHA-256 fingerprint and
    installs it into this machine's trust store. The installer itself stays your user;
    only this step asks for more. On macOS the authority goes into your login keychain,
    and macOS asks for your password. On Linux it is copied into the system anchors
    through `sudo` for one command. Firefox profiles get it through `certutil` when it
    is installed; otherwise the step tells you to set
    `security.enterprise_roots.enabled`. If you cancel the prompt, the install still
    completes and reports *not trusted yet* with the manual command; `bun run dev`
    serves either way. On macOS a cancelled dialog leaves no certificate behind in the
    keychain. If this machine already trusts the authority, nothing is asked.

    **Afterwards.** `bun run tls:renew` (`--force` to renew now) issues a new
    certificate from the same authority, so nothing needs to be trusted again.
    `bun run tls:untrust` removes the authority from every store the installer put it
    in. `--abort` removes what the aborted install added; if that removal is refused,
    it keeps the record in `../private/tls/` so `bun run tls:untrust` can finish it.

#### Fixed

- **The ontology tool's "set records" can no longer write a node into another TLD's namespace.**

    A record of `<tld>0` now only ever produces the node `<tld><id>`. A record whose TLD field
    names another TLD is reported and skipped instead of overwriting that TLD's node; the tool
    refuses sections that hold no ontology nodes (`test3`, `ontology1`, `localontology0`…) with
    `request.invalid_options`; in list mode the search must target exactly the tool's section, and
    a search with "recursive children" ticked is refused, because it would pick records the search
    did not select. On a TLD registry record (`ontology35`), a TLD that still has rows in
    `dd_ontology` but whose nodes drifted (for example only its root is left) is now re-derived in
    full, not just its root; a TLD already in sync only has its root refreshed, and a TLD with no
    rows stays empty — this action does not re-activate a TLD. See
    [tool_ontology](./development/tools/reference/tool_ontology.md).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-21-ontology-projection-guard`.

- **A developer install now installs the development dependencies `bun run dev` needs, and the development listener can serve HTTPS (`SERVER_TCP_TLS_CERT_FILE` + `SERVER_TCP_TLS_KEY_FILE`).**

    **Development dependencies.** The installer's bootstrap installs only its own,
    production dependencies, so after a developer install the first `bun run dev`
    crashed with `Cannot find package 'less'`. The developer route now has an
    `install_dev_dependencies` step (`bun install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`),
    run as the checkout's owner, that installs only what is missing; a checkout that
    already has them is left as it is. Production, Docker and Trial installs keep the
    production-only tree. If the step cannot reach the npm registry, the install fails
    and quotes bun's error. Run as root in a checkout another user owns, the step refuses.

    **HTTPS on the development listener.** Two new keys, `SERVER_TCP_TLS_CERT_FILE` and
    `SERVER_TCP_TLS_KEY_FILE`, give the `SERVER_TCP_PORT` listener a certificate: it then
    speaks HTTPS and the boot log prints an `https://` address. Set both or neither: a
    half pair, an unreadable file, a file that is not a certificate or a key of another
    certificate stops the server at boot (exit 78) with the key and path named. It never
    falls back to plain HTTP. While the certificate has less than 30 days left, every
    boot warns and names `bun run tls:renew`. Without the keys, nothing changes; without
    `SERVER_TCP_PORT` the keys are ignored. The test and update-drill servers always
    serve plain HTTP, whatever the pair in `../private/.env`. The
    warning for a listener opened to the network now says "no TLS" only when that is
    true.

- **A developer install now writes a development listener, so `bun run dev` serves the browser on port 3500.**

    **The listener is written.** A developer install used to write no `SERVER_TCP_PORT`,
    so `bun run dev` served only its unix socket and the browser reached nothing until
    the `.env` was edited by hand. The developer route now writes a *Development only*
    section: `SERVER_TCP_PORT` (default `3500`, `--dev-port`), `SERVER_TCP_HOST`
    (default `127.0.0.1`, this machine only; `--dev-host 0.0.0.0` opens it to the
    local network, and the Review and a headless run's summary warn), `DEDALO_DEV_MODE=true`,
    `DEDALO_DEBUG_API_ERRORS=true`, and the listener's certificate. The interactive
    installer asks these on a new **Development server** step.

    **The certificate.** `--tls` on the developer route is `local_ca` by default (a
    local certificate authority kept in `<private>/tls`), `none` (plain HTTP) or `files`
    (your own pair, with `--tls-cert` and `--tls-key`). `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE` is
    written to match: `true` over HTTPS, `false` over plain HTTP, where a browser on
    another machine would otherwise drop the login cookie.

    **A port in use is refused.** When another program already listens on the port,
    the Review does not offer `install`, and a headless run stops before writing
    anything; the refusal names the next free port. The installer never picks another
    port for you.

    **A re-run keeps your values.** The port, the address, a certificate pair and the
    two modes your `.env` already has are kept unless you answer them again, and the
    Review lists them as kept. A kept port or address that is not valid is refused
    like an answer, so you replace it with `--dev-port` or `--dev-host`. `--tls none` over a kept pair clears it. No other route
    writes any of these keys.

## 7.0.0-beta.6 — 2026-10-15

1110 commits: `git log --no-merges v7.0.0-beta.4..v7.0.0-beta.6`

!!! warning "Action needed when you update"

    - Dédalo now runs on Bun 1.4.3, which fixes a runtime defect that could leave a process waiting forever, at full CPU, on a program it had started.
    - Every AI request now counts against daily limits set per user and per profile, and generated answers need their own permission.
    - The browser installer is gone — install with the terminal installer; a server with no configuration now refuses to start.
    - SELinux lets the web server reach the Dédalo engine only, and no backup or rollback step runs as root on files the service user can change.
    - The terminal installer sets up the whole host: production, Docker and trial install in one run.
    - The site builder's OpenCode driver loads only the configuration the site builder states.
    - A site builder agent turn can no longer leave configuration in its home directory for the next turn to read.
    - Thesauri are offered from one exported manifest, hierarchy.json, and nothing but declared dependencies is pre-selected.
    - The PostgreSQL socket you give the installer is now the one the server connects through (`DB_SOCKET`).
    - Docker installations now pull a published, signed Dédalo image, or build it locally if you prefer, and record the choice in `.dedalo.env`.
    - Installations now choose their domain ontologies (Oral history by default) and install what each one declares it depends on; the install database carries only the core ontologies and no test data.
    - "The Publication API v1 on a publication host answers again: its configuration names the release that runs."
    - New installations are connected to the official update server and always have the Languages thesaurus; a server restarted by systemd or Docker must now declare `DEDALO_SUPERVISED=true`.
    - "A publication host can now be installed with one guided command, `provision init`, on Debian, Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, and RHEL, Rocky or Alma 9 and 10 with SELinux; the Publication API v1 runs in a FastCGI pool of its own."
    - The publication host provisioner now refuses an instance declaration that anyone other than root could change.
    - Publication host provisioning works with Apache on Debian and Ubuntu.
    - Several publication hosts on one server are checked for isolation.
    - The site builder's Claude Code agent no longer loads configuration from the site's own files, and refuses a Claude Code that cannot be told not to.
    - The site builder's agent can no longer choose its own agent program, read another site's activity, or stall a turn with a planted brief.
    - A site's AI turn no longer runs commands planted in the site's git settings, and the site builder says why it refuses a run.
    - The site builder runs each site's AI agent as that site's own system user, from units that root installs. systemd 248 is now enough, and `provision apply` must run before the updated daemon starts.
    - Only profiles granted the assistant tool can use the assistant.
    - The site builder can no longer start its agent units through polkit
    - Outbound fetches now refuse every IPv6 route to an internal address.

### For users

#### Security

- **Logging back in as another user no longer saves the previous user's pending edit.**

    When a session expires while you are working, Dédalo shows a login box over the page so you can sign in again without losing your work. Before, if a *different* user signed in on that box, the edit that was waiting to be saved was sent anyway — under the new user's name, so the Time Machine and the "modified by" stamp named the wrong person. Now a pending save, or a page section waiting to load, is resumed only when the same user signs back in. If someone else signs in, nothing is sent: the page reloads, and until it does nothing can be saved, deleted, moved or uploaded from it — only signing in again is allowed. Your unsaved edit stays marked as unsaved. The decision of who signed in is made in one place only, and the login box just passes the answer on, so the check cannot be weakened by changing one copy of it.

    The same now holds when the other user signs in somewhere else — in another tab or window of the same browser. Before, the next save from your page was quietly retried with the other user's session and recorded under their name. Now every answer from the server says whose session it is, your page keeps working only with your own session, and an answer from someone else's makes the page reload instead of sending anything. A lock you held on a field is no longer released on the other user's behalf when such a page closes, either.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-session-user-beside-csrf-token`.

- **Rich text is cleaned by a real HTML parser when it is saved.**

    Text fields with formatting are cleaned of anything that could run a script when they are saved. That cleaning used to pattern-match the text, which missed some disguised forms (for example an encoded `javascript:` link or an event handler written without a space) and sometimes changed ordinary text that merely mentioned such words. It now reads the text the way a browser does: disguised forms are caught, and text and formatting that are not dangerous come back exactly as written. Embedded SVG, MathML, frames, `noscript`, `title` and `textarea` blocks are now removed together with their content, HTML comments are removed, an attribute written twice on one tag is kept once with its first value (the one a browser uses), and a tag left unfinished at the very end of a value is dropped, as a browser would drop it. The cleaning is repeated on its own result until nothing changes, so removing one dangerous piece can never join the text around it into a new one. Dropping it takes the same short time however long the unfinished part is; in the rare value where the end cannot be found that way, the whole value is kept as plain visible text rather than lost. Values saved before this update are not changed until they are saved again.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-rich-text-sanitizer-tokenizer`.

- **Searching or sorting by a field the user may not see no longer reveals its values.**

    A search on a field of the section itself (not of a linked record) did not check the user's permission on that field, so repeated searches like "starts with A", "starts with B" could reveal a hidden field's value, and sorting by it revealed its order. A filter or a sort on a field the user's profile hides now matches nothing and sorts nothing, and the request carries the usual "some content was not shown" notice. Fields shown to the user through a portal or an autocomplete they are allowed to use remain searchable there — and only there: the server checks that the portal really belongs to the section the request names and that the user's own profile grants it, so a request cannot borrow that allowance by naming some other portal, and the record information fields every user may search (created and modified date and user) stay searchable for everyone. Which section's permissions apply is decided by the records being searched, never by what the request says about them. A sort over several sections at once is applied only when the field is visible to the user in every one of them.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-09-30-search-root-step-acl`.

- **A search whose conditions are joined by OR at the top level no longer returns records outside the user's projects.**

    When every condition of a search was joined by OR (for example "title contains
    X **or** title contains Y"), one of the conditions was checked without the
    user's project restrictions and the other without the section being searched.
    A user limited to some projects could therefore see records of projects they
    do not hold. The conditions are now always kept inside those restrictions.
    Administrators without project restrictions see no difference.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-09-29-search-where-parts-parenthesized`.

#### Removed

- **Activity and Time-machine sections no longer offer a section toolbar**

    The **Activity** and **Time machine** sections are read-only system logs: every
    record is written by the engine and never edited by hand. They nevertheless used
    to show a section toolbar (export, import, print, update cache, …) whose buttons
    all act on records the engine refuses to modify.

    Both sections now ship an empty section toolbar, so the dead buttons are gone.
    The **Time machine** list also stops showing the collapse/expand buttons toggle
    that Activity had already dropped — the two now render the same search-only
    toolbar. Components *inside* these sections (for example the time-machine button
    on a historical value) are unaffected.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-06-consultation-only-no-section-tools`.

#### Changed

- **Checkboxes and radio buttons inside a tool now wear the tool's colour, not Dédalo orange**

    A ticked box or radio button inside a tool was filled with Dédalo's orange,
    whatever the tool — so a checkbox in a blue tool disagreed with the toolbar and
    header around it. The checked widget now takes the tool's own identity colour,
    the same colour its header edge and its action buttons use; the browser picks a
    tick that contrasts with the fill. Covers the tool body and the status controls
    on the tool header, so every tool follows automatically.

- **The user activity chart names actions in your language.**

    The *Activity by type* chart of a user's activity (Login, Save, Edit, Upload complete…)
    now takes its action names from the application's translated labels, in the language
    you are using, instead of from ontology terms. Saved statistics from earlier versions
    are read as before and add up with new ones under the same action. The seven
    activity-only names (login, logout, upload complete, recover section, recover component,
    stats, new version) are new labels, translated in every shipped language.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-12-user-activity-what-labels`.

- **Searching a thesaurus branch with all its descendants costs the same however large the branch.**

    Expanding a term to all its descendants (the "with children" search, fixed filters, the tree) used to ask the database once per term of the branch — about 1,650 requests for a branch of 1,200 terms. The whole branch is now read in one request, in one consistent snapshot, with the same result. Sibling terms that share an internal number across two sections are now always listed in the same order (by section) instead of an order that could change between reads.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-children-recursive-one-statement`.

- **The site builder now says why it refused, and which refusals clear by themselves.**

    Before, most refusals of the site builder tool read the same: "The site builder rejected the request". A site name already taken, a build still running, a site with no webspace, a server full of running agent turns and a missing confirmation all showed that one sentence, and none of them was marked as something to retry. Now each refusal has its own message: the name is taken, a folder for that name is still on the server, the domain belongs to another site, there is nothing to publish yet, the site has used its disk space, the server has reached its site limit, and so on. A refusal that clears by itself (another task is running on the site, too many agent turns at once) is reported as temporary, so you can try again in a moment. Permission refusals say that the site builder needs developer or administrator permission, or that the agent session belongs to another user.

    For API consumers: the tool's errors are new `site_builder.*` codes (listed in the wire contract entry), the busy family moves from `site_builder.rejected` (400) to `site_builder.busy` (503, retryable), and no site-builder error carries a free-text message any more — the code and its label are the message.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-site-builder-reason-codes`.

- **A failed agent turn in the site builder now says what went wrong, in your language.**

    Before, when an agent turn of the site builder failed, the chat showed the site builder service's own internal sentence — sometimes a server path, a user id or a raw program error — in English whatever your language, and nothing said whether trying again could help. Now each failure has its own message: the turn ran out of time, it was stopped (by you, or because the service was shutting down), the server could not prepare it, the agent stopped with an error (its own output is shown apart, as the agent's), the session history could not be read, or one of the refusals the site builder already explains (the site is busy, the server cannot run the agent safely, …). The details an administrator needs stay in the site builder's log.

    For API consumers: an error record of the `session_stream` event stream is now `{type:'error', error:{code, category, message, label_key, retryable}, agent_output?}`, and the stream's `event: error` frames carry the same error body — never free text. New codes: `site_builder.turn_timeout`, `site_builder.turn_interrupted`, `site_builder.turn_setup_failed`, `site_builder.agent_failed`, `site_builder.replay_failed`.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-11-site-builder-turn-error-frames`.

- **The tools of a section list are now grouped in one Tools menu.**
