- **Docker installations now pull a published, signed Dédalo image, or build it locally if you prefer, and record the choice in `.dedalo.env`.** *(action needed)*

    Until now every Docker installation built its own image from the checkout. Dédalo now publishes the engine image, signed, to its own registry and to mirrors — GitHub Container Registry and Docker Hub — and you choose where your installation takes it from ([where the image comes from](./install/docker.md#choose-where-the-image-comes-from)):

    - **One of Dédalo's registries.** The [registry table](./install/docker.md#dedalos-registries) says which ones publish today; the registry Dédalo runs itself is the primary, the other two are mirrors of the same images. A registry that is not yet available is never offered. Images are published per release, so until the first stable release is published, the installer builds locally.
    - **A registry of your own**, holding copies of the published images ([how to mirror them](./install/docker.md#a-registry-of-your-own)).
    - **A local build** from the checkout, with `-f deploy/compose.build.yml` ([a local build](./install/docker.md#a-local-build)).

    `./install.sh` asks the question, offers the registries that publish your checkout's version first, and builds locally when none does. With `cosign` installed it checks the image's signature ([checking the signature](./install/docker.md#checking-the-signature)). The answer is written to `.dedalo.env` as five keys — `DEDALO_COMPOSE_FILE`, `DEDALO_IMAGE`, `DEDALO_VERSION`, `DEDALO_IMAGE_MODE`, `DEDALO_IMAGE_VERIFY` ([the keys](./install/docker.md#the-dedaloenv-keys)) — and every later update takes the image from the same place. The compose files no longer build: they run `DEDALO_IMAGE:DEDALO_VERSION`. Updating is now one command, `./deploy/dedalo-image-update.sh --version <version>`, which takes a database backup, gets the image, re-pins `DEDALO_VERSION` and rolls back on its own if the new version does not come up healthy within the health timeout (15 minutes by default, so long boot migrations are waited for) ([upgrading](./install/docker.md#upgrading)); with signature checking on, it also refuses a signed image that is not the version it asked for. Going back after an update that succeeded is a short manual procedure ([rolling back by hand](./install/docker.md#rolling-back-by-hand)). Its old `--mode`, `--image` and `--tag` flags are gone.

    **Action for an existing Docker installation.** Add these lines to `.dedalo.env` (on the full stack, create the file with your three `POSTGRES_*` values as well), with the version your checkout declares:

    ```shell
    DEDALO_COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.simple.yml
    DEDALO_IMAGE=localhost/dedalo
    DEDALO_VERSION=7.0.1
    DEDALO_IMAGE_MODE=build
    DEDALO_IMAGE_VERIFY=none
    ```

    Then build once under the new name and recreate the stack:

    ```shell
    docker compose -f docker-compose.simple.yml -f deploy/compose.build.yml --env-file .dedalo.env build dedalo
    docker compose -f docker-compose.simple.yml --env-file .dedalo.env up -d
    ```

    (on the full stack, `docker-compose.yml` instead of `docker-compose.simple.yml`, in the file and in the commands). The first update of such an installation needs `--skip-version-check`. See [an installation from before the image pin](./install/docker.md#an-installation-from-before-the-image-pin).

- **A publication host on another machine installs from one kit file built on the work host.**

    Installing a publication host on a second machine no longer means copying five entries of the work checkout by hand. On the work host, `bun run hostagent:pack -- --draft <draft.json>` builds one archive — the agent's code with its production dependencies (installed for the kit, without the tests), the draft and the installer, with a list of every file's checksum — and prints its sha256. The same checkout and draft always give the same file. The kit carries no password and no token: those are typed or created on the publication host. There, `sh install.sh <instance> --kit <file> --kit-sha256 <sha256>` refuses a kit whose sha256 is not the one the work host printed, then refuses an altered, extra or missing file before any of its code runs. A draft the guided install would refuse is refused when the kit is built. Installing from a checkout (`--source`) is unchanged. See [the kit](./install/publication_host.md#the-kit).

- **After an install from a kit converges, `provision init` offers to remove the kit file it was given.**

    `install.sh --kit` now tells init which kit file it was given and the sha256 it verified. When the install converged, init asks whether to remove that file (the default is no); without a terminal, `-- --yes` removes it. Only that file is removed, and only while it still has the verified sha256: a replaced file or a link is left in place and named. Re-runs need no kit, and the work host can always build it again. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#the-kit).

- **Two-machine publication hosts pair from one sealed, passphrase-protected file.**

    At the end of a guided install on a publication host reached over TLS, `provision init` now writes one encrypted pairing package — the engine fragment, the agent's token and the engine's TLS bundle — readable by root only, and shows its one-time passphrase once on the terminal (it is stored nowhere, and without a terminal no package is written). On the work host, `dedalo:pair-publication-host add <name> --package <file>` asks for the passphrase without echo (or reads it with `--passphrase-stdin`), opens the package in memory and runs the same checks and the same live proof as before. A wrong passphrase or an altered file is refused before anything is contacted. Delete both copies of the package afterwards; `--decide pair.package=again` writes a new one. Pairing with the three loose files is unchanged, and a host on the same machine still pairs directly. See [Pairing](./install/publication_host.md#pairing).

- **"`provision init` reports the sealed pairing package as stale once the work host has used it, and removes it on request."**

    The sealed pairing package init writes on a two-machine install holds the agent's token and the work system's TLS key. Once the publication host's agent has recorded a command from the work host after the package was written, every later init run (and `--dry-run`) reports the package as stale and offers to remove it — the default on a terminal, `--decide pair.package=remove` without one, which also removes it earlier. Init removes only the file it wrote and records the removal in its journal; a later run reports the package as gone. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#guided-install).

- **A new publication host can be drafted, kitted and paired from the Publication hosts panel.**

    As the Dédalo root user, **Maintenance → Publication hosts → New publication host** now makes the draft for a new publication host: type the site's domain, choose one machine or two, and the panel proposes the instance, the accounts, the service and free ports, which you can change before saving. The draft is checked with the publication agent's own rules and against the other instances on the same machine, and a refusal names the field. For two machines the panel builds the install kit from the release the code updater verified, shows its sha256 and lets you download it; then, once the publication host is installed, you upload its sealed pairing package and type the passphrase there. The package must belong to that draft — its instance and the agent address inside it — and the agent must prove it live before anything is stored; the passphrase and the package are never kept. The command-line paths are unchanged. See [New publication host](./install/publication_host.md#new-publication-host).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-09-publication-host-panel-setup`.

- **A publication host whose declaration drops the Publication API v1 now has its v1 pool, log rotation and v1 files removed by `provision apply`.**

    Re-declaring an existing v1+v2 publication host as v2-only used to leave its v1 FPM pool, the pool's log rotation, the v1 API releases and configuration (with its database credentials) and the pool's own directory behind. `provision apply` now keeps a record of what it provisioned (`provisioned.json` in the instance's configuration directory) and removes what the declaration no longer has: the pool through the FPM configtest and a reload (a pool that was the install's only one is put back and apply stops), the rotation, and both v1 trees, after the agent restarted. `provision check` lists each removal first. Only files that still carry the provisioner's own stamp for that instance, and trees exactly as it left them, are removed; anything edited, unstamped, foreign or with another owner stops the run and is named. The v1 SELinux rules go with them; the v1 account stays. A pool that moves to another FPM version is retired the same way. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#guided-install).

- **A publication host can now serve the Publication API v2 only, without the Publication API v1.**

    The Publication API v1 is legacy: it is needed only by websites built for Dédalo v6. A publication host's declaration without a `v1` block now installs a v2-only site, the recommended shape for a new site: no v1 account, no v1 configuration file and no v1 runtime on the host, and the guided install (`provision init`) neither looks for nor asks about any of them. The draft chooses with `"apis": "v2_only"` or `"v1_and_v2"`, or by the presence of its own `v1` block, and a v2-only site names its distribution family in `site.os_family`. The work system never pushes a v1 release to such a host, and its **Publication hosts** panel shows the v1 row as *Not served*, which is not a fault. Existing hosts that declare v1 are unchanged. See [the publication host install](./install/publication_host.md).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-09-publication-host-v2-only-site`.

- **On Docker installations, the Update code panel now shows how to install each release, and can hand the update to an optional host updater.**

    On a Docker installation the code lives inside the image, so the panel cannot replace it in place. Until now it only said *Update blocked*. It now shows an **Image updates** block: where this installation's image comes from (pulled from a registry, and whether that registry is one of Dédalo's, or built on the host), and, for the release you select, the exact command to run on the Docker host, `./deploy/dedalo-image-update.sh --version <version>`. The in-container readiness checks are still listed, folded, because they describe the in-place update this installation does not use.

    You can also install the optional **host updater** on the Docker host (`sudo ./deploy/dedalo-image-updater.sh install-units`). It is off by default. With it installed, the panel offers **Request this update**: the host updater picks the request up within about a minute, runs the same command with its backup, health check and rollback, and the panel shows the outcome. A request needs the superuser and maintenance mode, and can only name a release on the normal upgrade path. The registry, pull or build, and the signature check are decided on the host, from `.dedalo.env`. The engine is never given control of Docker. See [the host updater](./install/docker.md#the-host-updater-optional).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-09-update-code-image-channel`.

- **The Update code panel shows each release's notes before you install it.**

    When you check for available updates, each published release now lists what it changes: its *Action needed* items and one line per change, the same ones this change log publishes for that release. You can read what an update will do before you choose it, on every installation. Developer builds and releases cut before this change have no notes. See [updating the code](./management/updates/updating_code.md).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-09-code-manifest-release-notes`.

- **The backup panel now says when backups are manual.**

    Dédalo never makes database backups on its own: a nightly job installed with the operating system does (see [Backups](./management/backup.md)). When no scheduled backup of the database has ever reached the backup directory, the *Make backup* panel in Maintenance now shows *No scheduler, backups are manual.*, with a link to the backup documentation. Before, it showed only the age of the newest backup, which looked like automatic backups that had stopped.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-08-make-backup-scheduled-evidence`.

- **On an nginx publication host, the media map is now pushed by Apply media rules, and shared safely by every instance on the host.**

    nginx's media rules need a small map in the server's `http {}` block (it checks the media login cookie and decides how SVG files are served). That map may be defined only once per server, but a publication host can carry several Dédalo instances, and until now it had to be placed and kept current by hand. On a publication host whose declaration sets `web.nginx_map: conf_d`, **Apply media rules** now sends this work system's map to the agent before the media rules. The agent never writes the file nginx loads: it hands its part to a small service that runs as root on the host, which checks every instance's part, merges them into one file, tests the configuration and reloads nginx. When every instance runs the same Dédalo version and media folder, the file is exactly the map Dédalo writes for a work host. The publication hosts panel shows the map's state for each host: the map expected and the map applied, the shared host map and how many instances it serves; a host whose map is out of date counts as drift. The host refuses, and the panel says why: a map that is not in the expected form, an instance whose media folders changed since its map was first accepted (the earlier map stays until `provision apply` is run for that instance), or another instance with a newer map than the host's renderer understands (the shared map is left as it is until `provision apply` is run for that newer instance). `provision init` sets `web.nginx_map: conf_d` when nginx includes `conf.d` inside `http {}` (the Debian and RHEL default), and moves a map placed earlier by hand into the shared one after you confirm. A host whose map is placed by hand (`web.nginx_map: none`, the default of a hand-written declaration) is not touched, and an agent too old to know the shared map is refused with a request to update it. Every configuration test and reload on a publication host, by the agent or by root, now waits for the others, so two instances can no longer reload the same web server at the same time; if the shared lock is missing, run `provision apply` for the instance.

- **"A publication host can now be installed with one guided command, `provision init`, on Debian, Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, and RHEL, Rocky or Alma 9 and 10 with SELinux; the Publication API v1 runs in a FastCGI pool of its own."** *(action needed)*

    `sh …/publication/host_agent/deploy/install.sh <instance> --source <checkout> --draft <file>`
    looks at the publication host, compares it with what the instance needs, prints what is
    already right, what it will change (with the exact commands and diffs) and what needs your
    decision, and changes nothing until you confirm. It creates the missing accounts, gives the
    site's home to root, downloads and verifies the site's Bun against a hash table taken from
    Bun's signed checksums, installs the agent's code, writes the declaration, provisions, adds two
    lines to the site's virtual host (with a backup, a configuration test and an automatic roll
    back), asks for the API database password on the terminal only, checks that the agent answers
    and pairs it with the work system on one machine (on two machines it prints the pairing
    commands to run on the work host). It never installs a package, never edits a
    FastCGI pool of yours, never sets an SELinux boolean or edits one of your files without a typed
    answer, and never runs on Ubuntu 22.04 (its polkit cannot read the agent's rules) or on RHEL,
    Rocky or Alma 8 (systemd 239 and kernel 4.18 are below what the units and Bun need: `install.sh`
    refuses EL 8 before it downloads Bun). Whoever can
    write the source it is given can become root through it: give it only a checkout you trust.

    On RHEL, Rocky and Alma with SELinux, `provision apply` now labels the instance's own paths and
    the v2 port, and the guided install asks before widening any SELinux boolean. A shared media
    directory is labelled for the web server only with your consent, kept in the declaration as
    `media.selinux_label: true` (the guided install writes it when you answer `act`). A typed
    secret (the database passwords, the v1 web user code) may not contain a space, `'`, `\` or `$`. The units need
    systemd 247 or newer: `provision apply` refuses an older one.

    The site's web server logs stay outside its home: in the home layout `provision apply` creates
    `/var/log/apache2/<domain>/` (RHEL `/var/log/httpd/<domain>/`, nginx `/var/log/nginx/<domain>/`),
    owned by root, and the rotation file `/etc/logrotate.d/dedalo_<instance>_web` (the distribution's
    own rotation does not reach a directory per site); point the virtual host's logs there. On Ubuntu
    26.04 a log under `/home` stops Apache from starting, and the guided install says so. The guided
    install reads the sudo policy the installed `sudo` uses (`/etc/sudoers-rs` under sudo-rs, when it
    exists), accepts a polkit that the system bus starts on demand, and asks for `e2fsprogs` when
    `chattr` is missing.

    The Publication API v1 now runs in its own FastCGI process pool, `dedalo_<instance>_v1`, under its own
    account, which the provisioner writes when the declaration names the new `site` block, with
    the site's web include beside it. A hand-run `provision apply` now waits for a running
    `provision init` of the same instance, and `provision check` answers exit 5 (busy) instead of
    drift while one runs.

    **Action needed on an existing publication host:**

    - create the host group every agent's service now runs with, once per host:
      `groupadd --system dedalo_pubhost`. Until then `provision apply` refuses and prints that line;
    - a declaration whose `v1.user` is `www-data`, `apache`, `nginx`, `www` or `nobody` (the old
      page allowed the web server's user with the web server's own module) is now refused: create an account for v1
      alone, give it the v1 configuration file (`chown <account>`, `chmod 0400`), declare it and the
      `site` block, and run `apply`. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#guided-install)
      and its manual steps 2, 3 and 9.

- **The Publication hosts panel now shows in red a publication server whose Bun differs from the version the work system pins.**

    Each host in **Maintenance › Publication hosts** has a new **Bun version** row, with the expected version (this work system's `.bun-version`) and the version the host reports side by side. It is green only when they are exactly equal, red on any difference (for example `1.4.2 != 1.4.3`), and unknown when the host cannot be reached or proved. The install guide now gives each site on a publication server its own Bun, installed by root in `/home/<site>/.bun/` at the pinned version, so each site can be upgraded on its own, and suggests naming each instance after its site's domain (`my-hosts.org` → `my_hosts_org`). See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#2-declare-the-instance).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-03-publication-hosts-widget`.

- **Several publication hosts on one server are checked for isolation.** *(action needed)*

    `provision check` and `provision apply` now read the other publication-host declarations on the
    server. They refuse an instance that shares a user (agent, v1 or v2), the v2 group, unit or
    port, a listening port, or a directory with another. Before, a shared user let one instance change the other's
    media rules and API releases, and a shared port only failed when the service started. When a
    runtime path (Bun, the v1 API's runtime) or the agent's directory is a link, the refusal now prints
    the real path to declare. The new section
    [Several instances on one server](./install/publication_host.md#several-instances-on-one-server)
    lists what each instance needs of its own.

    The installation page now declares the instance before creating its accounts, and gives the
    exact commands. `provision check` names each missing account with its declaration field and
    the command, in the order to run them. The new section
    [Lay out each site in its home directory](./install/publication_host.md#lay-out-each-site-in-its-home-directory)
    puts each site's state root beside its document root (`/home/<site>/dedalo`, with the home
    owned by root) and shows the virtual host that maps the APIs into the site.

    The examples' `v2.health_url` was `…/dedalo/publication/server_api/v2/health`, which answers
    404 under the v2 API's default `BASE_PATH`, so every v2 release would fail its health check.
    It is now `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/health`, which answers whatever prefix the API is published
    under; use that form in your declaration.

    **Action needed:** the declaration's `web.group` is replaced by `v1.user`, the user the
    Publication API v1 runs as: with one process pool per site, that site's pool user (the pools may
    share the web server's group). Write `"web": {"server": …, "unit": …}` and
    `"v1": {"user": …}`. The v1 configuration file in `shared/` must now be owned by that user and
    readable by it alone (`chmod 0400`): installing a v1 release is refused with
    `shared_config_exposed` otherwise. The agent, v1 and v2 users must be three different accounts.

- **A paired publication server now gets the Publication APIs matching the work system's version, can keep a verified copy of the published media, and is checked from the public side.**

    After every confirmed code update or code restore (a rollback to an earlier version), the work system sends the matching Publication API releases to each paired publication server, exactly as the update verified them. A database restore does not change the code and sends nothing; the panel shows any lag and **Push API releases** realigns it. A file changed on disk since then stops the push and is named in the panel. In **copy** mode the publication server keeps its own copy of the published media, only public qualities of published records. Unpublishing makes the files answer "not found" as soon as the publication server accepts the unmark (until it does, for example while it cannot be reached, the panel shows the deletion as pending and the files stay public), then deletes them, and the deletion counts as done only once the server's file list confirms it. The maintenance panel can also check each publication server through its public address: a published file must load and an unpublished one must not, after every rules change and on a schedule. On a copy server, where the unpublished file is normally absent, a "not found" proves nothing and the check says unknown, never a pass. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md).

- **The publication hosts panel shows each copy-mode host's media copy, and root can bring one host back in sync on demand.**

    For a publication server that keeps its own copy of the published media, the publication hosts panel now has a **Media copy** row. It reads OK when the copy matches what the work system publishes. It reads pending while files are still being copied or removed, and red when an unpublished file has not been confirmed deleted from the public server after one check period (ten minutes), or when the server stopped being a copy server while it still held files. The engine checks and repairs every copy server by itself every ten minutes, and right after a data restore. The root user can run it for one server at once with **Reconcile media copy**. Applying it by hand, here or from the **Reconcile** panel, is reserved to root. A server that cannot be reached is reported as a failure, never as done, and its pending deletions are completed on the next check. A copy server is now protected by the same media rules as a server that mounts the shared media (**Apply media rules** works for it too), so an unpublished record stops being served before its files are deleted.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-03-publication-hosts-widget`.

- **A separate publication server can now run a small agent that the work system pairs with, to install the Publication APIs, apply media rules and report status, without root access.**

    Institutions whose public website runs on its own server, or on its own hostname on the same server, can install the **publication host agent** there. It accepts a fixed list of requests from the work system and nothing else: report status, check the media mount, apply the web server's media rules (keeping the previous rules if the new ones fail the configuration test), and install or roll back a Publication API release (the previous release keeps serving when a new one is not healthy). The work system connects over mutual TLS, or over a local socket on a single server, and proves the pairing with a fingerprint. The agent runs as its own user with two narrow grants (the web server's configuration test; and reloading the web server, restarting the v2 API, and starting or stopping a scratch copy of the v2 API on a local port to test a new release), and the publication server never needs to download packages. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md).

- **A separate publication server can now serve published media from shared storage, with its own access rules.**

    Institutions whose public website runs on its own server, reading the same media storage as the work system (read-only), can now generate media rules for that server: `bun run media:publication-host-rules --root <mount>` (Apache, or nginx with `--server nginx`). The publication server then serves only the files of published records, in the public quality folders, and never accepts the work system's login cookie. Originals are never served. See *A separate publication server with shared media storage* in the media protection manual page.

- **The maintenance panel now shows each paired publication server, and can apply its media rules or roll back a Publication API release.**

    A new **Publication hosts** panel in Maintenance, in the Publication group, lists every publication server the work system is paired with. For each one it shows whether the server answers, whether the pairing still matches, its media mode and mount, whether its installed media rules are the ones the work system would generate now, and which Publication API releases are current. The root user can apply the media rules, check the media mount, roll back a Publication API release, edit a server's public address, quality folders and probe files, or remove a server; other administrators see the panel read-only, without the servers' network addresses. Servers are added only on the work server's command line (`bun run dedalo:pair-publication-host`), run as the user that runs Dédalo, from the files the publication server's provisioner writes; the token is given in the fragment, a private file or standard input, never as an argument. The pairing is proved before anything is saved, and the work system never sends its token to a server whose pairing fingerprint does not match. The **Media access control** panel links to it. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#pair-it-with-the-work-system).

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-03-publication-hosts-widget`.

#### Fixed

- **The Docker and Trial installers check, before you type `yes`, that the official image of your version is published — a beta has none, so choose Build.**

    Official Dédalo images are published for **stable releases only**: a prerelease (a beta) and a development checkout have no official image. Until now the Docker and Trial routes defaulted to the official image anyway, so on a beta an install that kept the defaults failed at `stack_image`, after `yes`, with every answer lost. The Review now asks the registry first (`docker manifest inspect`, then `docker buildx imagetools inspect` — nothing is pulled). When the image of your version is not published, the Review says so and does not offer to install; your answers are kept, so go back to the Image screen and choose **Build** (`--image-source build`) or a registry of your own. When the registry cannot be reached, the Review says it could not be checked and does not block the install. That check waits at most 15 seconds, shows `checking the official image …` while it waits, runs once per Review, and says what happened in plain words (the registry did not answer, or could not be reached) — Docker's own error goes to the install log. A local build or a registry of your own is never checked this way. See [official images are stable releases only](./install/docker.md#official-images-are-stable-releases-only).

- **Dédalo now runs on Bun 1.4.3, which fixes a runtime defect that could leave a process waiting forever, at full CPU, on a program it had started.** *(action needed)*

    On Bun 1.4.2, a process that had already run many synchronous calls to external programs could,
    now and then, wait forever on one that had already finished, at 100% CPU (Bun issue 34069). The
    server makes such calls for a few checks (the code update panel's git checks, the versions of the
    PostgreSQL tools, ImageMagick, ffmpeg and curl); the command-line tools and the test suite make
    many, which is where it was seen. Bun 1.4.3 fixes it, so the pinned runtime (`.bun-version`)
    moves from 1.4.2 to 1.4.3, and the update panel refuses this release until the server runs it.

    **Action needed, before you apply this update:**

    - **Host installation:** as root, install the verified 1.4.3 runtime at `/opt/dedalo/bun/1.4.3/bun`
      exactly as [the `host_runtime` step](./install/manual_install.md#manual-host_runtime) does (with
      `PIN=1.4.3`, checked against this release's `.bun-sha256`), point the instance's `ExecStart` at
      it ([the `host_units` step](./install/manual_install.md#manual-host_units)), run
      `systemctl daemon-reload`, restart the instance, then apply the update.
    - **Container installation:** nothing extra; the new image carries Bun 1.4.3
      ([Upgrading](./install/docker.md#upgrading)).
    - **Publication hosts:** each site's Bun must move to 1.4.3 as well, or its **Bun version** row
      turns red ([Upgrading a site's Bun](./install/publication_host.md#upgrading-a-sites-bun)).

- **Publication progress no longer runs past its estimate while a job is still working.**

    When a section links to other records of the same section (for example types
    related to other types), the publication job counted those linked records as part of
    the selection. The progress then passed its estimate ("Processing records 42206 of
    42137…", "estimate exceeded") while the job was still running. Progress now counts
    only the records you selected; linked records are still published as before.

- **The installer refuses an installed instance's name up front, and a refused Review checks again on install.**

    - **Production, an instance name already installed on the host**: the System check, right after the name, now says `instance <i> is already installed on this host (<registry file or drop-in>)` and asks for another name. The Identity check no longer calls that instance's account "an earlier install's leftover" to remove with `userdel`, and a typed service user that belongs to another instance gets that instance's clash, not the leftover advice. A fresh headless run over a complete install of the name says the same instead of "resume it or undo it".
    - **A refused Review**: pressing Enter (or typing `install` in `--plain`) measures the plan again; once the cause is fixed (a CA trusted, a port freed) it goes on to the `yes` prompt with every answer kept. The key bar says `enter check again` instead of `enter install`, and the untrusted-chain refusal says "check again" instead of "run this again".
    - **The first instance on a fresh host**: when the run installs nginx, the closing To-do now includes the note about nginx's own default site on port 80 (`/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default`).
    - **Resume after an interrupted Docker install**: the released-lock line says whether the earlier run was in a container or on a host.
    - **Docs**: `production.md` lists the update-server question before the domain ontologies, in the order the screens ask them.

- **The installer's System check edit, Review re-check and default-site note, salt hint and Docker abort messages now match what happens.**

    - **A failed System check**: the check asks no questions, so `edit` (`e` on the full screen, `edit` in `--plain`) now goes back to Install type, the screen whose answers it checked. Before, it only ran the check again. The prompt, the button and the key bar all say `edit (back to Install type)`.
    - **A refused Review checked again**: the `checking again…` line disappears when the check ends. Before, it stayed frozen under the `yes` prompt or next to the result. When nothing is refused any more, the installer says `checked again — nothing is refused now: install is offered`.
    - **The salt after a failure or a Ctrl-C**: once the engine steps have generated `DEDALO_SALT_STRING`, every ✖ block names the command that reads it back. The value itself is never printed there. Ctrl-C leaves the full screen, which was the only place that showed the salt. On docker and trial the command is now `docker compose … run --rm --no-deps dedalo grep ^DEDALO_SALT_STRING= /private/.env`, which works whether or not the stack is running. `docker.md`, `quickstart.md`, `production.md` and the installer reference describe this.
    - **Docker / trial `--abort`**: the undo names only the containers that exist, measured with `compose ps --all`. An install stopped before the engine started now says `no container of dedalo, nginx, backup was ever created`. The kept-images hint and its `docker image rm` command list only images present on the machine, checked with `docker image inspect`. Before, it named `nginx:alpine` even when that image was never pulled, and the command failed.
    - **Production, nginx installed by the run (Debian/Ubuntu)**: the Review's *To do* now says that the package's default site keeps port 80 (`port 80: the default site stays yours (/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default, default_server) …`). Before, this note appeared only after the run, on the Done card.

- **The installer names a killed engine and shows what the engine said while it stopped.**

    - When the engine steps' process or container is killed (for example out of memory, or
      `docker kill`), the installer's ✖ line now says so, e.g. "the engine container was killed by
      SIGKILL — out of memory, or a kill", instead of quoting a Docker Compose progress line such as
      "Container dedalo-install-engine Created".
    - After a Ctrl-C, the lines the engine prints while it stops (such as "ended the seed restore's
      database session") now appear inside the ✖ block, on both the full screen and the plain
      output. On the Docker routes they were lost before.
    - On a production install that uses the institution's own certificate, the packages step no
      longer lists certbot, which it does not install.

- **Installer: one interruption block on Ctrl-C, a resume that re-checks and tells everything, the salt on a terminal resume, and clearer screens.**

    - **Ctrl-C during a step that runs a child** (the engine steps, a build) ends as one *install interrupted* block with exit code 130 and the run recorded *interrupted* — never also an *install failed* block, or exit 1.
    - **A `--resume` that completes the install** shows the generated `DEDALO_SALT_STRING` when it runs on a terminal (the docs always said so; it printed only the command that reads it), and the closing block reminds you to keep it with your backups. Its closing *To do on this host* lists the notes of every step, the ones done in an earlier run included.
    - **A `--resume` after earlier steps ran again** (after an `--abort` of a served instance) probes the public address again instead of trusting the old result; every resumed step says whether it was *verified again* or had *nothing to re-check*, and a resume of a complete install says `install already complete — every done step that has a check was verified again`.
    - **A refusal is worded `refused:`**, never *install failed* — for example `--abort` of a sealed install. An `--abort` that keeps a served instance now closes its run record.
    - **The ontology's RETIRED-property notices** (for ontology authors) no longer reach the operator's terminal during an install.
    - **Screens:** the Install type starts on Production, the recommended route; an unsupported system ends with *This system cannot run this route — quit, or go back to choose another route*; a failed check is marked ✗ on the step rail; the System check's warnings stay in view under the next screen, drawn with `!` and `✗`; `back` re-asks the question you left and runs the check again; a re-check before the Review names the answer that changed it; yes/no switches need Enter; the Review's `w` says it writes the answers and quits. In plain mode the bootstrap's dependency install draws no progress bar (`--no-progress`).

- **"Production and by-hand installs: one backup directory from the first run, another web server refused, and an abort that tells a started instance from one that never started."**

    - **`--engine-only --backup-dir`** (the by-hand host procedure) now checks and creates the backup directory it writes to `.env` (`DEDALO_BACKUP_DIR=<backup dir>/db`) from the first run. It used to create `<private>/backups/db` instead, and a `--resume` after an interruption then stopped at `check_directories`. When that check fails, it now names the directory.
    - **Another web server is refused before any change.** The Production System check refuses a run whose ports (80 and 443, or yours) another program holds, such as another instance's nginx when Apache is chosen, and a run that would install a second web server beside the installed one. The Review's *To do* list names the program before you type `yes`.
    - **An abort after an interruption inside `host_first_boot`, before the unit was started,** now removes the instance completely. It used to count the instance as served and keep its user, database and code for removal by hand.
    - **An abort interrupted during `host_packages`** names only the packages and repositories the host really has as kept, never a package the run did not get to install.
    - **A failed or interrupted `--engine-only` run** says to run the same command again with `--resume` or `--abort`, instead of printing a `bun run scripts/install.ts` command that would run as root with other answers.
    - **A resume says what it did with each step already done:** checked again (`verified again: …`) or nothing to check, instead of "skipped".
    - **The Review** marks a directory that already exists on its own `mkdir` line (*exists: not created*).
    - **Install by hand ([manual_install.md](./install/manual_install.md)):** the host check reads `/etc/os-release` in a subshell, so it no longer overwrites the page's `$NAME` (the public address) with the distribution's name. The host record's `nginx_map_owner` is rendered from what `host_web_site` did. The site file's header names both the installer and the page. Both chain-trust failures that `openssl verify` prints are named. Its *One web server* check now says what the installer refuses: installing one web server beside the other, and any other program on the ports; a host with both already installed goes ahead.
    - **[Removing an instance](./install/multi_instance.md#removing-an-instance):** take the backup before any `--abort` (a direct `pg_dump` is given for after one), clear the failed units, and remove the instance's web logs and timer stamps. The steps an abort already did are marked.
    - **[Production](./install/production.md):** the `host_engine` Verify enters the `0750` install folder as the service user, so it no longer fails with *Permission denied*.

- **An install interrupted during the database restore can be resumed or undone at once, and the host shows the engine's own refusal.**

    - **Ctrl-C during the seed restore (Docker route above all)**: the restore's database session could outlive the removed engine container on the PostgreSQL server for about two hours, and until then `--resume` and `--abort` refused with `a seed restore into '<db>' is still running`. Now a Ctrl-C ends the restore's session before the installer exits (on Docker the engine container is given time to stop itself before it is removed). A `--resume` or `--abort` that holds the database's install lock ends a restore this install left behind, says so (`⚠ ended the seed restore an interrupted run left on '<db>' …`) and goes on. A restore that belongs to another install is still refused and left alone. Every installer database session also asks the server to drop it within about a minute if its client disappears.
    - **The engine's reason in the host's ✖ line**: on the docker, trial and production routes, a refused or failed engine child is now quoted (`the engine steps failed: <its reason> — …`, `the engine child refused its --abort: <its reason> — nothing before it was undone`). Before, the reason was lost, and the abort said "see above" with nothing above.
    - **Docs**: [troubleshooting](./install/troubleshooting.md#resuming-and-undoing-an-install) lists both refusals; the [installer reference](./install/installer_reference.md#resuming-an-install-resume) explains how an installer's own leftover restore is ended.

- **Docker and trial installs: the local image build reports the release version, nginx always publishes its ports, and a resume re-checks the site.**

    - **A local image build at install time** now goes through `deploy/dedalo-image-build.sh`, the builder the image updater already used: a clean snapshot of the checkout's last commit, so uncommitted and untracked files never reach the image, `/health` reports the release version (never `X.Y.Z.dev`), and the image carries its own version and commit labels instead of the Bun base image's. The Review shows that command.
    - **nginx is recreated on every start of the stack** and must publish every port it declares. After a start that failed because another program held port 80 or 443, a `--resume` used to reuse a container that came up with no port and report the install complete; it now recreates it, or names the port it cannot publish.
    - **A `--resume` probes `/health` again** (on the engine's socket and through the published address), even when an earlier run recorded the probe done, so a stack started again is never reported complete without a check.
    - **An institution certificate whose chain this machine does not trust** is listed on the Review under *TO DO*, before you type `yes`, instead of being refused only after every answer was given.
    - **Removing an install:** a served `--abort` names the images it keeps and points to the route's own removal section — the new [Removing the stack](./install/docker.md#removing-the-stack) on the Docker route — and both removal sections now say how to reclaim the images, the build cache and the installer's Bun caches. The build-time estimate is one figure everywhere (about 2 to 6 minutes on 2 CPUs).

- **Every installer front end ends with the same *To do on this host* list, the salt's read command in it.**

    The full-screen installer's Done screen had no *To do on this host* list: the firewall command, the outside check and the other notes flashed by during the run and were gone. The Done screen now lists them (and leaves them on your normal screen when it closes), as the line mode and `--resume` runs do. On Production, Docker and Trial the list also names the command that reads the generated `DEDALO_SALT_STRING` back, on every run that completes the install — also a `--resume` after an earlier screen had already shown it.

- **Docker and Trial installs probe the media gate again on resume, and name their images and locks correctly.**

    A `--resume` that starts the stack again (after an `--abort`, or a stopped stack) now runs every `stack_health` probe again, the media gate included, instead of `/health` only. A locally built image carries Dédalo's own `source`, `url`, `description` and `licenses` labels instead of empty ones. On a completed install, `--abort` no longer suggests `docker image rm postgres:18`, because PostgreSQL keeps running on that image. A resume after an interrupted run says in plain words that the earlier run's lock was released, with no warning sign. An untrusted certificate chain is refused on the Review, before `yes`. The Docker and Trial pages now give the exact command that reads the salt back, say the salt is not shown again by a later `--resume`, and include `node_modules` in the removal steps. The installer reference says `--image-version` also applies to a local build.

- **The full-screen installer's closing lines start on a clean line, and the manual removal list covers Bun and a gpasswd after an abort.**

    When the full-screen installer ends (done, failed or interrupted), the closing `✔` or `✖` lines now start at column 0 and nothing of the screen is left beside or under them, also on terminals that do not support the alternate screen (`screen` without altscreen, a serial console, a session recording). The manual list for removing an instance ([Removing an instance](install/multi_instance.md#removing-an-instance)) now removes the instance's Bun runtime under `/opt/dedalo/bun/<pin>/` when no other instance uses that pin, and says that `gpasswd` exiting 3 after an `--abort` is harmless.

- **Installer re-checks, interrupts and messages say things once and at the right moment.**

    A check made stale by a later answer (the Identity check, once the web server is chosen) runs again right after that step, not at the end. `back` from a failed System check and forward again runs it again, its rows printed once. Ctrl-C during the engine step prints one interruption block. The System check's ok rows say their result once (`ok  Bun  runtime 1.4.3`), the short Docker and Trial check stays visible on the next screen, a typed `quit` in line mode prints the closing line, an unknown word at a failed check gets a plain sentence, the Review's local-build line says how long the build takes, and the Trial's Review points at the Trial page's firewall warning.

- **A Production install interrupted before its server ever ran is removed whole by --abort, and the production pages match what the installer does.**

    On Production, an instance now counts as served only when its unit has actually run or the engine answered. Before, an interruption a few milliseconds into the first start, before the unit ever ran, was treated as served, and `--abort` kept its user, database and code to be removed by hand. Now `--abort` checks systemd and the socket first and removes such an install completely. An `--abort` that removes the service user first removes what that user left at the top of `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` (Bun's `bun-node-<hash>` directory and `.<hash>-0.hm` marker), so no file of a removed account is left behind; the dependency install also keeps its temporary files inside the instance's tree. When the firewall already allows the ports, the closing *To do on this host* list no longer mentions it; the System check line still reports it. The [Production](./install/production.md) page lists the questions in the order they are asked, adds `sudo` to the Verify commands that read inside the install folder and the socket directory, and points to the salt's read command. [Removing an instance](./install/multi_instance.md#removing-an-instance) now says where the backup is written before step 7 deletes it, warns that copies made with `cp -a` keep the service user as owner, and gives the `gpasswd`, `userdel` and `groupdel` commands. [Install by hand](./install/manual_install.md) defines `render` where it is first needed, and its unit loop stops instead of writing empty files when `render` is missing. It also shows the full `--status --json` answer and says that a tree built from a checkout reports a `.dev` version.

- **The installer says what its system check would refuse on the Review, before `yes`, and a refusal never loses your answers.**

    An untrusted certificate chain, Apache beside a running nginx, an image version other than the installer's, or a port already in use were refused only after you typed `yes` — and every answer had to be typed again. The Review now measures the same system check the run makes and lists what it refuses as errors; install is offered once they are fixed. The **Image version** field refuses a tag other than the installer's own (or its `-dev` tag) at once, and the Docker and Trial check refuses a published port something else already listens on. If the check still refuses at `yes`, the session stays on the Review with your answers; if the run is refused after it started, before it changed anything, your answers are written to an answers file and the command that runs them again is printed. See [Installer reference › Interactive mode](./install/installer_reference.md#interactive-mode).

- **A Docker installation that builds its image here now updates from a clean snapshot of the release, like the install**

    On an installation whose image is built on the host (`DEDALO_IMAGE_MODE=build`), `deploy/dedalo-image-update.sh` used to build the new image straight from the checkout. Every untracked file in it went into the image, and the engine then reported its version as `X.Y.Z.dev` even though the image was tagged `X.Y.Z`. An update now builds the way the installer does, with the same builder (`deploy/dedalo-image-build.sh`). It takes a snapshot of the release commit with `git archive`, builds the image from that snapshot, then deletes the snapshot. The image holds only committed files and reports the release version and its commit date. Changes to tracked files are still refused before the update starts. A tree without git is now refused with a sentence that says why, instead of failing halfway through. If you build an image by hand, use `./deploy/dedalo-image-build.sh "$PWD" localhost/dedalo:<version>`. See [a local build](./install/docker.md#a-local-build).

- **The official Dédalo image carries Dédalo's own url, description and licence labels.**

    The published image set only its title, source, revision, version and creation date, so `docker inspect` showed the base image's url, description and licence, or none. It now carries the same `org.opencontainers.image.source`, `url`, `description` and `licenses` values as an image built locally by the installer, read from one shared definition.

- **On the Docker and trial routes, `--abort` removes an install interrupted before the engine container ever started, database included.**

    The installer counted a Docker or trial instance as *served* — a live instance that `--abort` never takes apart — as soon as `stack_up` began, before the `dedalo` container had started. An install stopped at that moment (a Ctrl-C, a failed `up -d dedalo`) was then kept by `--abort` as if it had served. Whether it served is now measured, as on the production route: the container started, or the engine answers `/health`; when that cannot be read, the instance is kept. An instance that never served is removed whole by `--abort --confirm-database <db>`. See [Resume and abort](./install/installer_reference.md#resuming-an-install-resume).

- **The publication tool shows every publication of a section, including two that share a database definition.**

    When two publications reach the same table through their own *database alias* pointing at one shared database definition (for example a production and a pre-production web), the publication tool showed only the first one, so the second could not be published from the tool. Each publication now has its own panel, with its own database, connection status and *Publish* button.

- **An interrupted or stopped install now resumes, an abort says exactly what it undid, and an instance that never served can be removed completely.**

    - **A resume restarts what stopped.** When PostgreSQL, the Docker stack or the instance's unit stopped after the installer started it (a reboot, `docker compose stop`, an abort of a live trial), `--resume` starts it again. Before, it refused with "changed outside the installer; --abort and start again", even though nothing had been changed.
    - **"Start again" now says what `--abort` costs.** Every message that suggests aborting says that `--abort` deletes the database the install created, unless the instance has already served.
    - **An instance that never served is removed completely.** Until `host_first_boot` starts the instance's unit, no request has reached it, and `--abort` now takes it apart whole: its engine install, its database, its user, its folders and its record. The engine undoes its own install only after two checks pass: the installer states that the instance never started, and the database still holds exactly the rows it had when the install sealed it. Once the instance has served, `--abort` still undoes only the host steps after the engine. The failure hint and the closing sentence say which case applies, and *Removing an instance* (several instances page) lists what to remove by hand.
    - **An abort cleans up after itself.** It removes the empty media tree the install created. It keeps the service user while that user still owns a file under the instance's paths, because a removed uid is given to the next account created on the host. On the Developer route it removes the state file and the session store the install created.
    - **The closing sentence of an abort is built from what it undid.** "Nothing was undone" is no longer followed by "removed: its site, units, user…". On Docker and the trial, the abort uses the stack's own words and lists the images it keeps; the engine's own "the database itself is kept" no longer appears before the host removes the database volume.
    - **The generated salt is shown once by the run that completes the install**, including a `--resume` that finishes an engine run that went on alone after its parent stopped. When no terminal can show it, the run prints the command that reads it back. It is never written to a log.
    - **The engine child stops with the installer.** It no longer goes on alone when the installer is killed, and a `--resume` refuses while a child of an earlier run is still working. On Docker, an interrupted run removes the engine's container.
    - **`--resume` asks only for the passwords a remaining step needs.** An engine run that already set the root password does not ask for it again.
    - **A refused System check leaves nothing behind.** An unsupported system or an instance folder that already exists stops the run before any record is written, and no resume or abort is offered. `--plan --route production` runs the same checks and reports them in `errors`.
    - **Quieter, truer installs.** The System check no longer creates `../private` (`ts_state.json`, the session store). The engine checks the backup directory the instance's units write to, not a second one under `private/`. Tools that never call the server no longer print "no server module". The Docker image creates the media root with mode `0750`, so the `mode_differs` warning is gone. An `--engine-only` run ends with the systemd pointer, and an interactive install records `"execute": true`.

- **The Docker and Trial installs now start a working nginx, publish only what they serve, and say why a check failed.**

    - **Docker route:** the generated nginx site includes the media rule files where the engine writes them (`/srv/dedalo/media/dedalo_media_protection*.nginx.conf`). Before, it named files that did not exist in the container, and nginx restarted forever.
    - **`stack_up` waits for nginx to stay up.** It checks that nginx is running, is not restarting, and accepts its configuration. If not, the step fails and quotes nginx's `[emerg]` line, instead of reporting "the stack is up".
    - **`--abort` of a completed install keeps PostgreSQL running.** It removes only the `dedalo`, `nginx` and `backup` containers (and `certbot`), so `--resume` can start them again. The abort also names the images it keeps.
    - **An untrusted certificate is refused early.** On the Docker route, an institution certificate whose chain this host does not trust is refused at the System check, which names its issuer and how to install the CA. A failed `stack_health` probe says why: for example, `the certificate chain is not trusted by this host`.
    - **The trial publishes plain HTTP only:** no port 443 and no certificate volumes. This needs Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer.
    - **A local image build shows each build step as it runs.**
    - **The backup container stops cleanly** on `docker compose stop` instead of being killed (exit 137).
    - **The Docker and Trial pages** now cover installing Docker per distribution (Podman is not supported), the `docker` group, the bootstrap tools (`curl`, `unzip`, `git`), the firewall bypass of published ports, and how to read `DEDALO_SALT_STRING` from the volume. The `dc` helper is now `ddc`.

- **The Production install now completes on RHEL 10 with SELinux, says before the install what you must do yourself, and keeps an unknown address away from every instance.**

    - **RHEL 10 with SELinux enforcing:** the socket's file context is written in the spelling the host's policy accepts (`/run/dedalo-<i>(/.*)?`). Before, `semanage` refused the `/var/run` spelling and the step could never pass. `--abort` now removes only the contexts the host really defines.
    - **The firewall is checked, and the fix printed.** The System check, the Review and the closing *To do on this host* list say whether firewalld's default zone or ufw lets the instance's ports in. When they do not, they print the command that opens them (for example `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https && firewall-cmd --reload`). The installer still never changes the firewall.
    - **The Review starts with a *To do* list** of what the installer checks but never does: the firewall, the Apache modules (`a2enmod … && systemctl restart apache2`, now also when the installer itself installs Apache on Debian or Ubuntu), and an institution certificate that expires within 30 days or that this server does not trust. Directories that already exist are marked *exists, used as is*.
    - **An institution certificate this server does not trust is refused at the System check**, naming its issuer and how to add the authority to the system trust store. Before, the install failed at its last step after 90 seconds with "got no answer". A failed public probe now says why (for example, `the certificate chain is not trusted by this host`).
    - **An address no site declares no longer reaches an instance.** On nginx, the first instance on ports 80 and 443 writes `dedalo-00-default.conf`, a site that serves nothing and comes first; a `default_server` of yours stays the default, and the last instance's `--abort` removes it. On Apache, each instance's site answers any other name with `421 Misdirected Request`.
    - **Each instance's database is its role's alone:** `CONNECT` and `TEMPORARY` are revoked from `PUBLIC`, so another instance's role can no longer connect to it.
    - **Installing from a `git` clone works under `sudo`.** `install.sh` installs its dependencies as the clone's owner (root writes nothing in your clone, and nothing in `/root/.bun`), and `host_runtime` archives the checkout without changing any `git` setting. `--route production` on an unsupported system is refused before anything is downloaded.
    - **A second instance on the same Bun pin** no longer reinstalls the runtime the first one is running. The release tree stays `0750` after extraction.
    - **Clearer refusals:** a clash with another instance is said once, naming every file that records it, instead of once per file. An unsupported system shows one sentence, the same as the troubleshooting page. On ARM servers the processor row no longer warns. On the Developer route, a `psql` older than the database server is flagged.
    - **The Production, manual-install, several-instances and web-server pages** cover the certificate trust requirement, the firewall commands, installing from a checkout, the explicit `--media-access-mode` for a hand install, `sudo` on the Verify commands, the files-mode certificate checks, and `ocrmypdf` being unavailable for `aarch64` in EPEL 10.

- **A tch install no longer asks for crm, a local image build reports its real version, and a production instance keeps its backups in one place.**

    - **No false "install it too" warnings after the ontology import.** References from an ontology's external-ontology mapping (`tch` maps itself to CIDOC CRM, `crm`) are no longer reported: only the RDF import reads that mapping. References into a thesaurus that the same install creates (for example `dc`), and references from a branch that no tree reaches, are not reported either. A warning that remains now says that the nodes using the missing ontology do not work until it is installed, and to add it only if you use them.
    - **A local image build reports the version it is tagged with.** The Docker and Trial routes build from the checkout's last commit (`git archive`), as the production route installs it. `/health` and the page footer show `7.0.0` and the commit date, not `7.0.0.dev`. Changes you have not committed are not in the image.
    - **One backup directory per production instance.** The installer writes `DEDALO_BACKUP_DIR=<backup dir>/db` to the instance's `.env`, the directory the backup units write. The server's own backups and its directory check use it too, instead of a second `<dir>/private/backups/db`. Install by hand: pass `--backup-dir "$BACKUP_DIR"` to the engine step.
    - **Install by hand, Apache:** the name guard now escapes the dots of the address, as the installer does (`@@SERVER_NAME_RE@@`).
    - **Docs:** the socket health checks in Upgrading and Migrating from v6 use `sudo`, because the socket directory is the service group's. The Docker page says that `SERVER_TCP_PORT` listens on the container's loopback unless `SERVER_TCP_HOST` is set.
    - **Tests:** the suite declares its own languages (the same as CI) instead of the ones in your `.env`, so a fresh install that declares two languages no longer turns about 25 language gates red.

- **The installer's screens now say what each route does, take a typed `yes` everywhere, and write `--write-answers` at the Review.**

    - **The trial asks no HTTPS port**, and its HTTP port is described as plain HTTP. Its acknowledgement now says what the documentation says: for an evaluation only, never real records.
    - **An acknowledgement takes a typed `yes` on the full screen too**, as in plain mode; Space still ticks it. The screen says how, in its own words.
    - **A pre-filled answer is replaced by the first key you type**, so the entity name no longer reads `museoMuseo de prueba`. Enter keeps the default.
    - **`--write-answers` works on an interactive run.** The file is written at every Review whose plan is valid, so quitting there keeps it. A session that ends before a valid Review says the file was not written.
    - **The Review speaks for the route.** Its "same as" line and the next step after `write <path>` give the route's own command (`sudo sh install.sh` on production, `sh install.sh` on Docker and Trial). "Install now" says whether the image is pulled and verified, pulled from your registry, or built here. The Docker and Trial Review no longer shows the production text about packages. The engine is handed only the passwords the plan uses.
    - **The Ontologies screen is in English and shows each heading once.** Group names come from the installer's language, every typology is one group, and the typology groupers (`hierarchytype`, `hierarchymtype`) are no longer offered.
    - **The System check says each row's state once** (`warn: Processor unknown`, not `warn: warn`). An unsupported operating system offers only quit, or back to another route, never "Retry". A check that passes moves on with its rows headed by its name.
    - **One step count.** Plain mode's `Step n of N` and the full screen's rail count the same steps. A created production database asks only its name: the role is the service user, with no host, port or password.
    - **The thesaurus advice of an interactive run** points to the Thesauri step and to Maintenance › Install hierarchies, never to command-line flags. The trial's To-do gives this machine's address, not `localhost`.
    - **Smaller fixes:** the header of an interrupted install no longer says "nothing installed yet"; the route cursor starts on the `--route` default; an empty password field breaks no rule until you type; plain mode's bootstrap output is uncoloured; the footer no longer shows `null` for a development build.
    - **The installer reference, the troubleshooting page and the installation hub** describe the real screen order, the System check rows per route, the firewall and own-CA cases, `restart` after `a2enmod`, the salt on `--resume`, and what `--abort` keeps once an instance has served.

- **The installer's System check no longer fails on a host without PostgreSQL**

    On a freshly installed server (no PostgreSQL client yet), the **System check** screen of `sh install.sh` failed with `the system probe failed unexpectedly (Error)` and still printed **System ready.** beside it. Now:

    - **Production** shows the PostgreSQL client as `ok` when it is absent — the installer installs PostgreSQL 18 itself — and warns when a client of another major is present.
    - **Docker** and **Trial** no longer check a host PostgreSQL at all; they show the **Docker**, **Compose** and **Disk** rows instead, with the same sentences the install's own check uses.
    - **Developer** shows a failed row with the fix: this route installs into an existing PostgreSQL and needs its client.
    - **System ready.** appears only when nothing failed. A check that could not run says so, with the error's class, its first line and the file holding the full text, to report.

    See [The System check screen](./install/troubleshooting.md#the-system-check-screen).

- **The installer no longer leaves Bun's cache in an existing hosting account's home.**

    On the Production route, the commands the installer runs with Bun as the service user (the dependency install, the engine steps, the migration check) now set `HOME` to the install folder on their command line (`runuser … -- /usr/bin/env HOME=<install folder> …`). `runuser` resets `HOME` to the account's own home, so with an existing hosting account whose home is not the install folder, Bun's caches were written there. The Review screen shows the new form, and [Install by hand](./install/manual_install.md) uses the same commands.

- **The update-ontology warning no longer claims your local ontology will be deleted.**

    The **Update ontology** panel and its confirmation dialog warned that the update would "delete the actual ontology" and that "you will lose all changes made to the local Ontology". That is not what the process does: it replaces the ontology of the TLDs you select (the common/shared ontologies) with the master's version and re-processes them. Your local ontology — custom TLDs and `localontology` overrides — is a different namespace and is kept, re-applied automatically when the updated nodes are processed. The panel note, the lead text, the submit label and the confirmation dialog now say so, in every interface language (the confirmation dialog was previously an untranslated English string; it is now a translated label). The only way the local ontology is replaced is if you explicitly add `localontology` to the list of ontologies to update — keep it out.

    Wire contract: `WC-2026-10-10-update-ontology-confirm-text`.

- **The PostgreSQL socket you give the installer is now the one the server connects through (`DB_SOCKET`).** *(action needed)*

    The installer's socket answer (`--db-socket`) was used by the installer's own connection test and then written as `DEDALO_SOCKET_CONN`, a key the server never read: an installation reachable only through the socket passed the install and then connected to `DB_HOST` instead. The answer is now written as the new key [`DB_SOCKET`](./config/config_db.md), and one rule decides the route for everything that connects to the database: the server, the installer's test, the nightly backup and the maintenance tools. When `DB_SOCKET` is set it wins over `DB_HOST`, and a socket that does not exist fails loudly instead of quietly falling back to `localhost`. An existing `.env` that holds `DEDALO_SOCKET_CONN` keeps working: it is now read as the old spelling of `DB_SOCKET`, so check that the directory it names is where your PostgreSQL socket really is before updating. A re-run of the installer writes the value once, under the new name. If you use the nightly backup unit, update `deploy/dedalo-backup.service` from the release so its database backup connects the same way.

- **On Docker, the browser client now always matches the engine that is running.**

    The proxy used to serve the browser client straight from the checkout on the host, while the engine ran from its image. When the two came from different versions — a checkout at one release behind an image of another — the client and the engine no longer understood each other, and pages broke in ways that looked like engine bugs. Now the engine publishes the client of its own image into a `client` volume each time it starts, and the proxy serves it from there. An update or a rollback therefore moves the client together with the engine. No action is needed: the new compose files declare the volume. If you keep your own compose file, give the `dedalo` service `DEDALO_CLIENT_PUBLISH_DIR: /srv/dedalo/client` with the `client` volume mounted there, and mount the same volume read-only in `nginx` instead of `./client` ([the files](./install/docker.md#the-files-and-where-they-live)).

- **The installation guides now install the watchdog and rollback scripts, tell existing servers how to declare supervision, and give RHEL a complete systemd unit.**

    The non-Docker installation and update pages were brought in line with the installer and the shipped units.

    - **Watchdog and rollback scripts.** The shipped watchdog and rollback units run two scripts from `/opt/dedalo/bin/`, outside the code tree. No page said to install them, so a server set up from the manual alone had a watchdog failing with `status=203/EXEC` every 30 seconds and no automatic rollback of a failed code update. [Production step 10](./install/production.md#10-run-the-engine-under-systemd) now installs them, and [Upgrading](./install/upgrading.md) refreshes them after each update.
    - **Existing servers and supervision.** [Upgrading](./install/upgrading.md#3-check-that-the-unit-declares-supervision) has a new step that checks the installed unit for `Environment=DEDALO_SUPERVISED=true`, `SuccessExitStatus=75` and `Restart=always`, and adds what is missing with a drop-in. [Troubleshooting](./install/troubleshooting.md#updating) explains the *No supervisor declared* refusal. The installer's last line now names the supervised ways to start the server instead of `bun run start`, which cannot take code updates.
    - **RHEL.** The RHEL-based systems page (since folded into [Production install](./install/production.md)) gives a complete `dedalo-ts.service` ordered after `postgresql-18.service`. The shipped unit names `postgresql.service`, which does not exist there. The page also runs the installer the same way as the production guide, and keeps `DEDALO_PG_BIN_PATH` in `.env`.
    - **Several instances.** The [multi-instance](./install/multi_instance.md) template unit now carries `KillMode=process`, the wider start limit, the rollback hook and the watchdog. The watchdog script takes `--restart-unit` / `--rollback-unit`, so a templated instance can point it at its own units. Each site is installed with `--socket`, `--media-path` and `--media-access-mode` instead of appending keys by hand.
    - **Corrections.** The backup set is five stores (site-builder instances included). Without `--media-path` the media root defaults to `../private/media`. The installer keeps every `.env` key it does not own, including keys added before the install. An air-gapped installation can update its ontology from local files ([updating the ontology](./management/updates/updating_ontology.md#updating-without-a-network-air-gapped-installs)). `STRUCTURE_FROM_SERVER` and `DEDALO_SOURCE_VERSION_LOCAL_DIR` are documented as having no effect. The four language keys are documented as required, with no default. The configuration pages point at `install/sample.env` in the code tree for the current list of keys: `../private/sample.env` is the installer's copy and a code update does not refresh it. The [developer quickstart](./install/dev_quickstart.md) lists the supervised start scripts and the second-instance script.
    - **Key names in `.env`.** The installer now writes every key under the name the [configuration reference](./config/config.md) uses (`DB_NAME`, `DB_HOST`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_PORT`, `ENTITY`, `PROJECTS_DEFAULT_LANGS`, `APPLICATION_LANG`, `DATA_LANG`) instead of the older fallback spellings (`DEDALO_DATABASE_CONN`, `DEDALO_ENTITY`, …). Before, a `DB_HOST` you added by hand silently won over the answer you had just given the installer. A re-run over an existing `.env` replaces the old spelling with the new one, so no value is left under two names. The engine and the backup scripts still accept the old spellings, so an existing `.env` keeps working unchanged.

- **The install database is compiled from the repository and proven by a fresh install before it ships.**

    Maintenance → *Build database version* → *Build install version* refused with "not
    runnable on this engine", pointing at a maintenance dashboard that no longer exists. It
    now compiles `install/db/dedalo_install.pgsql.gz` — the database every fresh install
    starts from — from files in the repository only (the schema and its migrations, the
    core ontology release packages, the languages and hierarchy registry files, the default
    accounts), never from an installation's database, so it cannot carry one
    installation's data or mistakes into every new install. Before the file is replaced
    the result installs itself in a scratch database and is checked; the same command is
    `bun run seed:build`. The seed ships with a manifest that records what it was built
    from. See [the seed](./development/ts_install_internals.md#the-install-seed).

- **"**Probe media** on a new copy-mode publication host no longer reports a problem before anything is published."**

    On a copy host, the marker directory `.publication/pub/` is created by the agent with the first
    published record. Until then the probe reported it as missing, so the first probe after pairing
    said *found 1 problem(s)*. An absent marker directory is now zero published records on a copy
    host; on a shared host it is still a problem.

- **"The guided publication-host install now runs on RHEL 9 with SELinux enforcing and fapolicyd: the polkit rules directory, the SELinux tools and fapolicyd's trust are judged as EL ships them."**

    The first run of the EL install drill on a real RHEL 9.8 machine (SELinux enforcing) found three
    things the guided install got wrong there. `provision apply` refused every instance because EL's
    polkit package owns `/etc/polkit-1/rules.d` by the polkit daemon's account: that directory, as
    the package ships it, is now accepted (any other owner is still refused). init reported the SELinux
    tools missing because `/usr/sbin/restorecon` is a link to `setfiles` on EL: a link to a program
    now counts. With fapolicyd active, an untrusted Bun may not even read the code it runs:
    `install.sh` now stops before the hand-over with the one line that trusts its Bun, and init's
    `host.fapolicyd` prints the lines for the site's Bun **and the agent's code** (re-runnable: an
    existing entry is updated). See
    [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#rhel-rocky-and-alma).

- **"On RHEL, Rocky and Alma with SELinux, the Publication API v2 of a site installed in its home now starts: systemd may read its settings and its release links."**

    The first API v2 release pushed in the EL install drill never started. Under the home layout the
    v2 directory kept the home's own SELinux type, which systemd may not read, so neither the v2
    settings file (`v2.env`) nor the links to the current release and to the release being tested
    could be followed: every install was refused (`scratch_start_failed`). `provision apply` now
    labels `<home>/dedalo/publication_api/v2` `dedalo_publication_v2_t`, the publication host's own
    SELinux type, which systemd may only read and the web server may not read. The v2 services also start their entry with `bun src/index.ts` instead of
    `bun run src/index.ts`, which left links in the service's private `/tmp` that systemd could not
    remove at every stop (an SELinux denial each time). Run `provision apply` (or init) again on such
    a site. See [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md#rhel-rocky-and-alma).

- **"The guided install of a publication host now gives a working command for the newer AppStream runtime of the v1 API on RHEL, Rocky and Alma 10."**

    On EL 10 the guided install said that no `dnf` command installs a version of the v1 API's
    runtime other than 8.3 as the system one, and offered Remi only. RHEL 10.2 ships 8.4 in AppStream
    as alternative packages with the same files as the default ones. When the declared version is not
    installed, `host.fpm_install` now prints the `dnf install` line for those 8.4 packages (the
    FastCGI server and the command-line interpreter). When an older system version is already
    installed, the command has `--allowerasing`, and the item says that every pool of the system
    FastCGI server then runs the new version. Remi and the default 8.3 are still offered. The guided
    install has now been tested on RHEL 10.2 with SELinux enforcing, as well as RHEL 9.8. See
    [Publication host agent](./install/publication_host.md).

- **"On a publication host with fapolicyd's `allow_filesystem_mark = 1`, the agent keeps its right to reload the web server and start its services."**
